Savory pies.Shepherd's pie: Shepherd's pie is made with minced lamb under mashed potato, since shepherds tend sheep. The potato topping dates it to after potatoes spread across Britain in the 1700s.
Savory pies.Pork pie: The pork pie of Melton Mowbray has a bow-walled hot-water crust, and the filling is uncured grey meat. It earned protected status in the EU.
Savory pies.Chicken pot pie: Chicken pot pie is an American comfort classic, and its roots go back to Roman-era meat pies. Frozen pot pies were a big hit in 1950s U.S. freezers.
Savory pies.Steak and kidney pie: This British pub staple pairs beef with kidney in thick gravy. The kidney is why some people avoid it, but it adds a deep, earthy flavor.
Savory pies.Cottage pie: Cottage pie is the beef version of shepherd's pie, and the name appeared in the 1790s, when potatoes became a poor family's staple.
Savory pies.Tourtière: Tourtière is a spiced pork pie from Quebec, served at Christmas Eve réveillon. Cloves, cinnamon, and allspice flavor the filling.
Savory pies.Fish pie: British fish pie is a baked dish of white fish and smoked haddock in a creamy sauce, topped with mashed potato. Some cooks add prawns and hard-boiled eggs.
Savory pies.Spanakopita: Spanakopita is a Greek pie of spinach and feta in crisp phyllo. The name literally means spinach pie, and it is popular during Lent as well.
Savory pies.Meat pie: Australia and New Zealand treat the hand-held meat pie as a national food, and Australians eat millions each year. It is tied to sports grounds and footy matches.
Savory pies.Cheese and onion pie: Cheese and onion pie is a vegetarian staple of northern England, often eaten hot or cold with chips. Lancashire cheese is a traditional filling.
Savory pies.Apple pie: Apple pie is called as American as apple pie, yet apples are not native to America and the dish is English. Early pie recipes appear in the 1300s.
Savory pies.Pecan pie: Pecan pie is a Southern dessert of pecans in a sticky filling of eggs and syrup. Pecan is one of the few major nut crops native to North America.
Savory pies.Key lime pie: Key lime pie is Florida's official pie, made from tiny, tart Key limes. A true one is often pale yellow, not green, because the filling is not dyed.
Savory pies.Pumpkin pie: Pumpkin pie is a Thanksgiving staple, but most canned filling is actually made from a type of squash. Colonists baked early versions inside a hollowed-out pumpkin.
Savory pies.Cherry pie: Cherry pie is a U.S. classic, and Washington's cherry-tree legend is why it is linked to Presidents' Day. Tart Montmorency cherries are the usual choice.
Savory pies.Banoffee pie: Banoffee pie was invented in 1971 at The Hungry Monk restaurant in Sussex. Its name merges banana and toffee, and the dish is a pie with no baking.
Savory pies.Mince pie: Mince pies are a British Christmas treat, and the filling, called mincemeat, now has no meat in most recipes. Suet is the one meaty ingredient that often remains.
Savory pies.Lemon meringue pie: Lemon meringue pie is a sweet pie of lemon curd topped with toasted meringue. It is a staple of mid-century American diner dessert cases.
Savory pies.Shoofly pie: Shoofly pie is a Pennsylvania Dutch molasses pie. Legend says its name comes from having to shoo away flies from the sticky filling.
Savory pies.Mississippi mud pie: Mississippi mud pie is a chocolate dessert said to look like the muddy riverbank of the Mississippi. It usually has an Oreo-style crust.
Savory pies.Boston cream pie: Boston cream pie is really a cake, not a pie, with custard filling and chocolate glaze. It was created at Boston's Parker House hotel and is Massachusetts's official dessert.
Savory pies.Blueberry pie: Blueberry pie is a summer dessert made from a berry native to North America. Wild blueberries are smaller and more intense than the cultivated kind.
Savory pies.Sweet potato pie: Sweet potato pie is a Southern dessert with deep roots in African American cooking. It is similar to pumpkin pie but smoother, and it is a Thanksgiving staple.
Savory pies.Rhubarb pie: Rhubarb pie uses a vegetable stalk as fruit, and the leaves are poisonous. A U.S. court once ruled it a fruit in 1947 to cut import tariffs.

Drinks that contain caffeine.Coffee: The world's most popular caffeine source. Beans are really seeds from coffee cherries, and a typical cup has about 80 to 100 milligrams.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Black tea: It carries caffeine, roughly half a cup of coffee's worth, which is why it can feel gentler.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Green tea: It has caffeine, though less than coffee, and also contains L-theanine, which many people say softens the buzz.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Coca-Cola: Its name came from coca leaf and kola nut, and a 12-ounce can has about 34 milligrams of caffeine.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Red Bull: A small 8.4-ounce can has about 80 milligrams of caffeine, about the same as a cup of coffee.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Yerba mate: A South American holly infusion with caffeine, the national drink of Argentina and Uruguay.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Espresso: A shot has about 60 to 70 milligrams of caffeine, less than a full mug of drip coffee, even though it tastes stronger.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Dr Pepper: A Texas soda from the 1880s, with caffeine, and one of America's oldest soft drinks.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Mountain Dew: Its caffeine content is among the highest of mainstream sodas, and it began in Tennessee as a whiskey mixer.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Cold brew: Steeped for hours in cold water, it often has more caffeine per serving than hot coffee, because of its higher concentration.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Pepsi: Created by a North Carolina pharmacist in 1893, as Brad's Drink, and it has caffeine.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Matcha: Since you drink the entire ground leaf, matcha delivers more caffeine than a cup of ordinary green tea.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Rooibos: A South African herbal tea, naturally free of caffeine, so you can drink it at bedtime.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Chamomile tea: A caffeine-free flower infusion, traditionally used as a calming bedtime drink.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Sprite: A lemon-lime soda that is caffeine-free, unlike many cola rivals, and the world's top-selling lemon-lime brand.
Drinks that contain caffeine.7 Up: A lemon-lime soda free of caffeine. It was created in 1929 and first sold as Bib-Label Lithiated Lemon-Lime Soda.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Ginger ale: A ginger-flavored fizzy drink, normally caffeine-free, and a traditional remedy for upset stomachs.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Lemonade: Sweetened lemon water, with no caffeine and a very old history, since it was sold on Cairo's streets in medieval times.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Orange juice: No caffeine, only fruit sugar and vitamin C, and a glass uses around two or three oranges.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Milk: It has no caffeine, and is often added to coffee to soften its bitterness.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Peppermint tea: A herbal infusion, naturally caffeine-free, so not a true tea.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Hibiscus tea: A tart herbal drink from flowers, free of caffeine and served hot or cold.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Coconut water: The clear liquid inside young coconuts, naturally caffeine-free and high in potassium.
Drinks that contain caffeine.Apple juice: It has no caffeine, and its sugar content is similar to that of many sodas.

Words for a baby animal.Cygnet: A young swan. The word comes from the French for swan, and cygnets are usually grey-brown until they mature.
Words for a baby animal.Fawn: A baby deer, spotted at first. Fawns are nearly scentless and stay still while their mother feeds nearby.
Words for a baby animal.Joey: A baby kangaroo, wallaby or other marsupial. The word is Australian, and a joey stays in the pouch for months.
Words for a baby animal.Foal: A baby horse, donkey or zebra. Foals can usually stand within an hour and run within a few hours of birth.
Words for a baby animal.Leveret: A young hare, born fully furred with open eyes. Unlike rabbit kittens, leverets are born in the open, not in burrows.
Words for a baby animal.Gosling: A baby goose. Goslings can walk, swim and feed themselves within a day, and they imprint on the first moving thing they see.
Words for a baby animal.Owlet: A baby owl. Owlets are covered in fluffy down, and their eyes face forward, even at a young age.
Words for a baby animal.Kit: A baby fox, ferret, beaver or rabbit. Fox kits are born with dark brown fur that changes to red as they grow.
Words for a baby animal.Calf: The young of cows, whales, elephants, and more. A blue whale calf is the largest baby on Earth.
Words for a baby animal.Tadpole: A baby frog or toad, living in water with gills and a tail. Frogs go through a complete metamorphosis.
Words for a baby animal.Piglet: A baby pig. Newborn piglets are born with sharp teeth, and often have a specific teat they stay with.
Words for a baby animal.Duckling: A baby duck. Ducklings can swim within hours, and they follow the first thing they see move, usually their mother.
Words for a baby animal.Drake: A male duck. The word also meant dragon in old English, and it's a trap as it is not a baby animal.
Words for a baby animal.Doe: An adult female deer, rabbit or goat, so not a baby. Female kangaroos are also sometimes called does.
Words for a baby animal.Ewe: A mature female sheep. A ewe can usually recognise her own lamb by smell and voice.
Words for a baby animal.Mare: An adult female horse, aged four or more. A young female horse is a filly instead.
Words for a baby animal.Stallion: An adult male horse that has not been gelded, so not a baby. Stallions often lead herds in the wild.
Words for a baby animal.Sow: An adult female pig, which can raise a litter of a dozen or more piglets. It is not a baby.
Words for a baby animal.Boar: A male pig, or a wild pig. Wild boars are a big part of European folklore, and not a baby term.
Words for a baby animal.Gander: A male goose. The word also gives us the phrase take a gander, meaning to look, from the stretching of a goose's neck.
Words for a baby animal.Buck: A male deer, rabbit, or goat. Antlers fall off the buck every year and regrow.
Words for a baby animal.Ram: An adult male sheep. Rams butt heads at speeds up to about 30 km/h, and some have big curled horns.
Words for a baby animal.Vixen: A female fox, though the word is also used for a spirited woman. She is an adult, not a baby.
Words for a baby animal.Cob: A male swan. A female is a pen, and the word cob also means a type of sturdy horse.

Venomous animals.Cobra: Cobras flare their hoods to look bigger, and a king cobra's venom can be strong enough to threaten an elephant.
Venomous animals.Rattlesnake: Rattlesnakes sense prey's body heat with pits between the eye and nostril, and baby ones can bite with full venom.
Venomous animals.Scorpion: Scorpions glow bright blue-green under ultraviolet light, and a few species can survive for a year without food.
Venomous animals.Black widow: Only female black widows are dangerous, and their venom is said to be many times stronger than a rattlesnake's by weight.
Venomous animals.Box jellyfish: The box jellyfish has 24 eyes and a sting among the most deadly in the sea.
Venomous animals.Stonefish: Stonefish are the most venomous fish known, and they sit camouflaged on reefs, looking just like a rock.
Venomous animals.Platypus: The male platypus has a venomous spur on each hind leg, making it one of the very few venomous mammals.
Venomous animals.Gila monster: Gila monsters, along with the Mexican beaded lizard, are the only venomous lizards in the US, delivering venom through grooves in their teeth.
Venomous animals.Honeybee: A honeybee's sting is barbed, so it often dies after stinging a mammal, unlike wasps, which can sting repeatedly.
Venomous animals.Wasp: Wasps can sting repeatedly because their stingers aren't barbed, and some paper wasps recognise one another's faces.
Venomous animals.Blue-ringed octopus: Tiny but deadly, the blue-ringed octopus carries tetrodotoxin, the same poison as pufferfish, and has no antidote.
Venomous animals.Cone snail: The cone snail harpoons its prey with a venomous dart, and its venom has given rise to a painkiller drug.
Venomous animals.Python: Pythons kill by constriction, not venom, and the longest, the reticulated python, can exceed six metres.
Venomous animals.Boa: Boas squeeze their prey rather than poison it; some species give birth to live young.
Venomous animals.Anaconda: Anacondas are among the heaviest snakes, but they are constrictors with no venom and spend most of their time in water.
Venomous animals.Poison dart frog: Poison dart frogs are poisonous, not venomous: toxins come from skin and from the ants they eat, not a bite.
Venomous animals.Pufferfish: Pufferfish are poisonous, not venomous; their tetrodotoxin is dangerous to eat but is not injected.
Venomous animals.Hedgehog: Hedgehogs aren't venomous; they use spines for defence and sometimes spread frothy saliva onto them, an odd habit called anointing.
Venomous animals.Monarch butterfly: Monarchs are poisonous, not venomous, thanks to toxins from the milkweed that they ate as caterpillars.
Venomous animals.Alligator: Alligators have a bite among the strongest of any living animal, yet carry no venom.
Venomous animals.Crocodile: Crocodiles rely on a bite force of around 3,700 psi, not venom, to subdue prey.
Venomous animals.Cane toad: Cane toads are poisonous, not venomous: toxin oozes from glands behind their eyes when threatened.
Venomous animals.Great white shark: Great white sharks have no venom; they rely on rows of serrated teeth that get replaced throughout their lives.
Venomous animals.Gorilla: Gorillas have no venom or poison; they rely on size, and their chest-beating is more of a display than a fight.

German foods.Bratwurst: Germany has hundreds of regional sausages, and Nuremberg's are tiny and grilled over beechwood in sets of six or more.
German foods.Sauerkraut: Fermented cabbage, which sailors, including Captain Cook's crew, carried on long voyages because the vitamin C kept scurvy away.
German foods.Pretzel: Its knotted shape is said to have been invented by monks, and the dough is dipped in lye before baking to give a dark crust.
German foods.Spätzle: Soft egg noodles pressed or scraped into boiling water; the name means 'little sparrows', and they are a staple in Swabia.
German foods.Currywurst: Sausage cut up and drenched in curry ketchup, which Berlin snack-bar owner Herta Heuwer said she invented in 1949.
German foods.Black Forest cake: Chocolate cake layered with cherries, cream and kirsch, named for the cherry brandy from the region, not for the forest itself.
German foods.Stollen: A dense fruit bread dusted in sugar at Christmas, and Dresden holds a stollen festival every year, where a huge loaf is paraded.
German foods.Sauerbraten: A pot roast marinated for days in vinegar and spices, and often described as Germany's national dish.
German foods.Weisswurst: A white veal sausage from Munich, traditionally eaten before noon, and, according to tradition, never after the bells of midday.
German foods.Rouladen: Thin slices of beef rolled around bacon, onion, mustard and pickle, then braised in gravy.
German foods.Lebkuchen: Spiced honey gingerbread, a speciality of Nuremberg for centuries, and a fixture at Christmas markets.
German foods.Kartoffelsalat: Potato salad, whose southern German version uses vinegar and broth, while the northern one tends to use mayonnaise.
German foods.Goulash: A paprika-spiced stew from Hungary, though it is also popular in Germany, so it's not originally German.
German foods.Pierogi: Polish filled dumplings, often served with fried onions and sour cream, so not German.
German foods.Borscht: A beetroot soup associated with Ukraine and Eastern Europe, not Germany.
German foods.Raclette: Swiss melted cheese scraped onto potatoes, so not German.
German foods.Fondue: Swiss melted cheese eaten from a shared pot with long forks; losing your bread in it traditionally earns a forfeit.
German foods.Haggis: A Scottish dish of offal and oats, not German.
German foods.Paella: A Spanish rice dish from Valencia, cooked in a wide shallow pan, so it is not German.
German foods.Moussaka: A Greek layered dish of aubergine, minced meat and béchamel, so not German.
German foods.Poutine: A Canadian dish of fries, curds and gravy, not German.
German foods.Risotto: Italian rice stirred slowly with stock until creamy, so it is not German.
German foods.Croissant: Austrian-style kipferl inspired the French croissant, but today it is a French pastry.
German foods.Pavlova: A meringue dessert from Australia or New Zealand, not German.

Landmarks in China.Great Wall: Built over many centuries by successive dynasties, its total length including branches is over 20,000 kilometres, though it isn't visible from space.
Landmarks in China.Forbidden City: Beijing's palace complex has nearly 1,000 buildings and housed 24 emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties, closed to commoners for centuries.
Landmarks in China.Terracotta Army: Thousands of life-size clay soldiers were buried with the first emperor Qin Shi Huang, and each face is unique. Farmers found them in 1974.
Landmarks in China.Li River: This river near Guilin flows past towering karst peaks, a view that appears on China's 20 yuan banknote.
Landmarks in China.Yellow Mountains: Huangshan is famed for twisted pines, sea-of-clouds views and granite peaks, and it inspired countless Chinese ink paintings.
Landmarks in China.The Bund: Shanghai's riverfront promenade is lined with early 20th-century European-style banks, facing the futuristic Pudong skyline across the Huangpu.
Landmarks in China.West Lake: A lake in Hangzhou celebrated in poems and paintings for a thousand years, long considered an ideal of Chinese landscape.
Landmarks in China.Summer Palace: The imperial garden in Beijing centres on Kunming Lake, and its long painted corridor is decorated with thousands of paintings.
Landmarks in China.Temple of Heaven: Emperors came to this Beijing complex to pray for good harvests, and its round Hall of Prayer was built without nails.
Landmarks in China.Three Gorges Dam: The world's largest hydroelectric power station on the Yangtze, holding back a reservoir that stretches about 600 kilometres.
Landmarks in China.Zhangjiajie: The sandstone pillars of this park inspired the floating mountains in Avatar, and its glass bridge draws many visitors.
Landmarks in China.Angkor Wat: The vast Khmer temple in Cambodia is the world's largest religious monument, and it appears on the Cambodian flag.
Landmarks in China.Taj Mahal: The white marble mausoleum in Agra, India, was built by Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, and took about 20 years.
Landmarks in China.Mount Fuji: Japan's iconic volcano rises about 3,776 metres, and has been a sacred mountain for centuries, last erupting in 1707.
Landmarks in China.Ha Long Bay: Vietnam's bay of thousands of limestone islands, whose name means descending dragon, is a UNESCO site.
Landmarks in China.Petronas Towers: The twin skyscrapers in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, were the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004.
Landmarks in China.Borobudur: A 9th-century Buddhist temple in Java, Indonesia, the world's largest, with over 2,600 relief panels.
Landmarks in China.Bagan: A plain in Myanmar dotted with thousands of temples and pagodas built between the 11th and 13th centuries.
Landmarks in China.Gyeongbokgung: Seoul's grand palace dates to 1395, and the changing of the guard is a popular show, so it belongs to Korea.
Landmarks in China.Marina Bay Sands: Singapore's hotel whose three towers are topped by a boat-shaped sky park with a massive rooftop infinity pool.
Landmarks in China.Wat Arun: The Temple of Dawn in Bangkok is decorated with colourful porcelain, rising above the Chao Phraya river.
Landmarks in China.Fushimi Inari: A Kyoto shrine with thousands of vermilion torii gates winding up a mountain, not found in China.
Landmarks in China.Kinkaku-ji: Kyoto's Golden Pavilion is covered in gold leaf, and a monk burned it down in 1950, inspiring Mishima's novel.
Landmarks in China.Chocolate Hills: In the Philippines' Bohol, over a thousand grass-covered mounds turn brown in the dry season, giving them their name.

Places in Peru.Machu Picchu: This Inca citadel at about 2,430 metres was abandoned and unknown to outsiders until Hiram Bingham made it famous in 1911.
Places in Peru.Cusco: The ancient Inca capital, whose name may mean navel of the world, has Spanish churches built on Inca stone walls.
Places in Peru.Lima: Peru's capital sits on a desert coast with almost no rain, but its cuisine is now celebrated around the world.
Places in Peru.Lake Titicaca: The world's highest navigable lake, at about 3,800 metres, shared with Bolivia, and home to floating reed islands.
Places in Peru.Nazca Lines: Enormous drawings of a hummingbird and monkey scratched into the desert, remarkably preserved by the dry climate.
Places in Peru.Arequipa: The White City is built of pale volcanic stone and sits below the cone of El Misti volcano.
Places in Peru.Sacred Valley: The fertile valley near Cusco was the Inca heartland, with terraced fields, salt pans at Maras and fortresses.
Places in Peru.Rainbow Mountain: Vinicunca's striped hillside, with colours from different minerals, rose to fame after ice melted to reveal it.
Places in Peru.Colca Canyon: One of the deepest canyons on Earth, often said to rival the Grand Canyon, and a famous place to watch Andean condors ride thermals.
Places in Peru.Iquitos: The largest city that can't be reached by road, accessible only by boat or plane, in the Peruvian Amazon.
Places in Peru.Huacachina: A tiny oasis village around a lagoon in desert dunes near Ica, where tourists try sandboarding.
Places in Peru.La Paz: The world's highest seat of government, at about 3,600 metres, sits in Bolivia, not Peru.
Places in Peru.Quito: The capital of Ecuador, at 2,850 metres, has one of Latin America's best preserved colonial centres.
Places in Peru.Salar de Uyuni: Bolivia's vast salt flat, the world's largest, becomes a giant mirror after rain, and it holds much of the world's lithium.
Places in Peru.Galápagos: Ecuador's islands, where Darwin studied finches and tortoises, inspiring his theory of evolution.
Places in Peru.Bogotá: Colombia's capital sits high in the Andes, around 2,600 metres, and has a famous gold museum.
Places in Peru.Cartagena: A walled Colombian city on the Caribbean coast, which was a key port for Spanish treasure ships.
Places in Peru.Patagonia: The windswept southern tip of South America, shared by Argentina and Chile, with glaciers and granite peaks.
Places in Peru.Iguazu Falls: Hundreds of cascades on the border of Argentina and Brazil, wider than Niagara, with the Devil's Throat.
Places in Peru.Easter Island: Chile's remote island of moai statues, over 3,500 kilometres from the South American coast.
Places in Peru.Tikal: The Maya city in Guatemala's jungle, not Peru, whose temples were shown in the first Star Wars film.
Places in Peru.Angel Falls: The tallest uninterrupted waterfall at about 979 metres, hidden in Venezuela's jungle.
Places in Peru.Santiago: Chile's capital sits in a valley ringed by Andes peaks, so it's not in Peru.
Places in Peru.Sucre: Bolivia's constitutional capital, known as the White City for its whitewashed colonial buildings.

Weather events (not geological).Tornado: A rotating column of air from a storm cloud; most are brief and small, but the strongest have winds above 300 km/h.
Weather events (not geological).Hurricane: Called a typhoon or cyclone elsewhere, it is the same storm; the name comes from Taino and Mayan words for a storm god.
Weather events (not geological).Blizzard: Defined by wind and visibility, not snow amount: sustained wind over 56 km/h and low visibility for at least three hours.
Weather events (not geological).Monsoon: From Arabic for season: it's a seasonal wind reversal, not just rain, and it feeds the farms of nearly a billion people.
Weather events (not geological).Hailstorm: Some hail in China and Bangladesh has reportedly killed people, and large stones can fall at over 100 km/h.
Weather events (not geological).Typhoon: Names a tropical cyclone in the northwest Pacific; Typhoon Tip in 1979 was the largest ever, about 2,200 km wide.
Weather events (not geological).Thunderstorm: Thunder is the shockwave from air heated by lightning; count seconds between flash and sound, and divide by three for kilometers.
Weather events (not geological).Heat wave: Often silent killers, they cause more deaths in many countries than any other weather event, since heat strains the body quietly.
Weather events (not geological).Drought: A slow, creeping event without a clear start; the 1930s Dust Bowl turned the US plains to dust and pushed farmers west.
Weather events (not geological).Sleet: In the US it's frozen raindrops; in Britain the word means a rain-snow mix, so the same word means different things.
Weather events (not geological).Derecho: A long-lived windstorm with straight-line winds as destructive as a tornado's, but spread over hundreds of kilometers, like in 2020 Iowa.
Weather events (not geological).Dust storm: A wall of dust can rise over a kilometer high; Saharan dust regularly drifts across the Atlantic to fertilize the Amazon.
Weather events (not geological).Earthquake: A trap: caused by shifting plates underground, so it is geological. Weather happens in the atmosphere.
Weather events (not geological).Tsunami: A trap: Japanese for harbor wave, caused by sea-floor movement, not by wind, so it is geological rather than meteorological.
Weather events (not geological).Volcanic eruption: A trap: powered by magma from within Earth, it counts as geology, although ash clouds can then alter weather worldwide.
Weather events (not geological).Geyser: A trap: Old Faithful erupts due to underground heated water, which is geothermal, not atmospheric.
Weather events (not geological).Aftershock: A trap: smaller quakes following a big one, so geological; they can continue for months or even years.
Weather events (not geological).Lava flow: A trap: molten rock from a volcano is geology; some flows move at a walking pace, others a snail's.
Weather events (not geological).Solar eclipse: A trap: an astronomical event of the Moon blocking the Sun. It affects temperature briefly, but it is not weather.
Weather events (not geological).Meteor shower: A trap: bits of comet debris burning up in the atmosphere are astronomical, and not weather, despite happening in the sky.
Weather events (not geological).Lunar eclipse: A trap: Earth's shadow falling on the Moon is astronomy, and clouds can only block your view of it.
Weather events (not geological).High tide: A trap: driven by the Moon's pull, tides are astronomical forces, though storm surges on top of them are weather.
Weather events (not geological).Supernova: A trap: an exploding star far away is astronomy; the one seen by Chinese astronomers in 1054 left the Crab Nebula.
Weather events (not geological).Pyroclastic flow: A trap: a fast avalanche of hot gas and ash from a volcano, so geology; it destroyed Pompeii and Herculaneum in 79 AD.

Cold-blooded animals.Snake: Snakes are ectotherms, so they bask to warm up. A large meal can ramp up a python's metabolism so much that it generates its own heat.
Cold-blooded animals.Lizard: Lizards bask on sunny rocks to raise their body temperature. Some desert species shuttle between sun and shade to stay at the ideal level.
Cold-blooded animals.Frog: A cold-blooded amphibian whose body heat follows the surroundings. The wood frog survives winter with much of its body frozen solid.
Cold-blooded animals.Goldfish: Goldfish take on the temperature of the water around them. They can survive icy ponds, as long as a patch of water doesn't freeze solid.
Cold-blooded animals.Crocodile: Crocodiles are cold-blooded, so they sunbathe in the morning. Their large size helps them hold on to heat and slow their cooling.
Cold-blooded animals.Turtle: Turtles are ectotherms, and many hibernate underwater. Some can absorb oxygen through the skin around their rear end during the winter.
Cold-blooded animals.Salamander: An amphibian that depends on external warmth. Some species can regrow lost limbs, and even parts of the heart and brain.
Cold-blooded animals.Iguana: Iguanas bask in the sun to warm up. In the cold, they can become so sluggish that they have fallen from trees in Florida.
Cold-blooded animals.Spider: Spiders are cold-blooded arthropods, and their speed depends on temperature. Cold weather slows them to a crawl.
Cold-blooded animals.Octopus: Octopuses are cold-blooded, with three hearts and blue blood. They tend to live short lives, with most species lasting only a year or two.
Cold-blooded animals.Cobra: A cold-blooded venomous snake that depends on the sun to heat up. Its hood is a display used to look larger when threatened.
Cold-blooded animals.Toad: A cold-blooded amphibian that tends to have drier, warty skin. Toads can survive in drier habitats than most frogs.
Cold-blooded animals.Tortoise: A land-dwelling cold-blooded reptile. Some giant tortoises have lived beyond 150 years, making them among the longest-lived animals.
Cold-blooded animals.Penguin: Penguins are warm-blooded birds and keep body heat with dense feathers and fat. Emperor penguins huddle in groups to survive Antarctic winters.
Cold-blooded animals.Bat: Bats are warm-blooded mammals, though some let their temperature fall during hibernation. They're the only mammals that truly fly.
Cold-blooded animals.Whale: Whales are warm-blooded mammals, with thick blubber to keep in heat. They also breathe air and nurse their young.
Cold-blooded animals.Dolphin: Dolphins are warm-blooded mammals who keep a steady body temperature in cold seas. They breathe air through a blowhole.
Cold-blooded animals.Polar bear: A warm-blooded mammal with thick fur and a layer of fat. Its skin is actually black, which helps absorb heat.
Cold-blooded animals.Ostrich: The largest living bird is warm-blooded, with a body temperature near 39 degrees Celsius. Despite its size, it can sprint around 70 km/h.
Cold-blooded animals.Hummingbird: A warm-blooded bird with a hugely fast metabolism. At night, it can drop into a torpor, lowering its temperature to save energy.
Cold-blooded animals.Platypus: A warm-blooded mammal that lays eggs, though it keeps a cooler body temperature than most mammals. It also hunts with electric sensors in its bill.
Cold-blooded animals.Human: Humans are warm-blooded, holding body temperature around 37 degrees Celsius. We shiver and sweat to keep it steady.
Cold-blooded animals.Seal: A warm-blooded marine mammal. A thick blubber layer lets it thrive in icy waters without cooling down.
Cold-blooded animals.Owl: A warm-blooded bird of prey. Special feather edges silence its flight, and it can turn its head about 270 degrees.

Phases of the Moon.New moon: The Moon sits between us and the Sun, so its lit side faces away, and this is the best time to see faint stars.
Phases of the Moon.Waxing crescent: Waxing means growing; from the Northern Hemisphere the lit sliver is on the right.
Phases of the Moon.First quarter: Called a quarter because the Moon is a quarter through its orbit, even though half its face looks lit.
Phases of the Moon.Waxing gibbous: Gibbous comes from a Latin word for hump; it is more than half lit and still growing.
Phases of the Moon.Full moon: The Moon rises near sunset, and the full cycle from one full moon to the next takes about 29.5 days.
Phases of the Moon.Waning gibbous: Shrinking after full, and it rises roughly 50 minutes later each night.
Phases of the Moon.Third quarter: Identical to the last quarter: the Moon is three-quarters of the way round its orbit, and it rises around midnight.
Phases of the Moon.Last quarter: It rises around midnight and is up in the morning sky; seen from the north, the left half is lit.
Phases of the Moon.Waning crescent: A thin crescent before dawn, and the dark part still glows faintly from earthshine, sunlight bounced off our own planet.
Phases of the Moon.Blue moon: A trap: a blue moon is just the second full moon in a calendar month, roughly every 2.5 years, not a phase and not blue.
Phases of the Moon.Harvest moon: The full moon nearest autumn's equinox, which rises at nearly the same time several nights running, helping farmers.
Phases of the Moon.Blood moon: A reddish moon during a total lunar eclipse; it is an event, not a phase.
Phases of the Moon.Supermoon: A full moon close to its nearest approach, up to about 14% bigger than the smallest; it is popular, not a true phase.
Phases of the Moon.Strawberry moon: June's full moon, named by Algonquin peoples for the strawberry harvest.
Phases of the Moon.Hunter's moon: The full moon after the harvest moon, named for hunting season.
Phases of the Moon.Wolf moon: January's full moon, named in folklore for the howling of hungry winter wolves.
Phases of the Moon.Honeymoon: Nothing to do with phases; the word dates to the 1500s, and one old idea says it mocked love that wanes like the moon.
Phases of the Moon.Black moon: An informal name for a second new moon in one month; it is not a distinct phase.
Phases of the Moon.Moonrise: The Moon appearing over the horizon, and it rises about 50 minutes later each day.
Phases of the Moon.Moon pie: A marshmallow sandwich from Chattanooga, Tennessee, first sold around 1917.
Phases of the Moon.Moonwalk: A dance popularised by Michael Jackson in 1983, though the move is older; it is not a phase.
Phases of the Moon.Moonshine: Illegal home-distilled liquor, so called because stills were run by moonlight to avoid detection.
Phases of the Moon.Lunar eclipse: It can only occur at full moon, when Earth lines up between the Sun and Moon; it is an event, not a phase.
Phases of the Moon.Sailor Moon: A Japanese manga by Naoko Takeuchi launched in 1991, whose heroine Usagi Tsukino's name means 'moon rabbit'.

Living things that photosynthesize.Oak tree: A mature oak can have hundreds of thousands of leaves, and one large tree can move well over a hundred gallons of water on a sunny day.
Living things that photosynthesize.Grass: Many grasses, including corn and sugarcane, use a faster C4 photosynthesis that works better in heat, which helped grasslands spread worldwide.
Living things that photosynthesize.Algae: Algae and other water-dwelling photosynthesizers produce a large share of the oxygen in each breath you take, rivaling all forests.
Living things that photosynthesize.Seaweed: Seaweeds are algae with pigments beyond green, so many look red or brown. Those pigments catch the dim blue light that reaches deeper water.
Living things that photosynthesize.Cactus: Cacti open their pores at night to take in carbon dioxide and store it, avoiding water loss in the daytime desert heat.
Living things that photosynthesize.Moss: Mosses have no true roots and soak water through their leaves. They were among the earliest plants to colonize dry land, hundreds of millions of years ago.
Living things that photosynthesize.Fern: Ferns reproduce with spores, not seeds, and covered Earth long before flowering plants. Much of the coal we burn came from ancient fern forests.
Living things that photosynthesize.Cyanobacteria: These bacteria invented oxygen-producing photosynthesis over two billion years ago, and their waste gas transformed Earth's atmosphere.
Living things that photosynthesize.Kelp: Giant kelp can grow about half a meter a day, building underwater forests that shelter otters, fish and sea urchins.
Living things that photosynthesize.Phytoplankton: These tiny drifting organisms feed ocean food webs from krill to whales, and they're visible from space as swirling green blooms.
Living things that photosynthesize.Sunflower: Young sunflowers track the sun across the sky, a behavior called heliotropism. Mature flower heads usually settle facing east.
Living things that photosynthesize.Lettuce: Lettuce is roughly 95 percent water, and its leaves photosynthesize like any other plant's. Its cousin the sunflower belongs to the same family.
Living things that photosynthesize.Venus flytrap: It photosynthesizes like any plant, and traps insects for extra nitrogen because the boggy soil it grows in is poor in it.
Living things that photosynthesize.Mushroom: Mushrooms are fungi with no chlorophyll, so they can't make food from light. They absorb nutrients from decaying matter instead.
Living things that photosynthesize.Yeast: Yeast is a single-celled fungus, so it can't photosynthesize. It ferments sugar into carbon dioxide and alcohol, which is why bread rises.
Living things that photosynthesize.Sponge: Sponges are animals that filter food from water. Some host photosynthetic algae inside, but the sponge itself doesn't photosynthesize.
Living things that photosynthesize.Jellyfish: A jellyfish is an animal and cannot photosynthesize, though the upside-down jellyfish hosts algae in its tissues and sits in sunlight.
Living things that photosynthesize.Mold: Molds are fungi that feed on whatever they grow on. With no chlorophyll, they don't need light and thrive in dark corners.
Living things that photosynthesize.Earthworm: Earthworms eat decaying matter and soil, and some gardeners credit them with turning huge amounts of soil every year. No light needed.
Living things that photosynthesize.Truffle: Truffles are fungi growing underground in partnership with tree roots, not sunlight. Some white ones fetch thousands of dollars a pound.
Living things that photosynthesize.Amoeba: An amoeba is a single-celled organism that hunts and engulfs food. Some relatives get green by hosting algae, but amoebas themselves don't photosynthesize.
Living things that photosynthesize.Human: Humans get energy by eating, not light. The idea of a photosynthetic animal does exist: the sea slug Elysia chlorotica steals chloroplasts from algae.
Living things that photosynthesize.Penicillium: This mold gave us penicillin after Fleming noticed it killing bacteria in 1928. Being a fungus, it doesn't photosynthesize.
Living things that photosynthesize.Starfish: Starfish are animals that eat mussels and other prey, pushing their stomach out to digest it. They have no chlorophyll.

Films set largely in space or on another.Gravity: Alfonso Cuaron's 2013 film unfolds almost entirely in orbit, and it won seven Oscars.
Films set largely in space or on another.Apollo 13: The real line was Houston, we've had a problem. The film changed it to the better-known have a problem.
Films set largely in space or on another.Alien: The 1979 film's creature was designed by H. R. Giger, and the Nostromo is a mining ship.
Films set largely in space or on another.The Martian: Andy Weir first self-published the novel online. The film's Mars was shot in Jordan's Wadi Rum desert.
Films set largely in space or on another.WALL-E: The first half hour has almost no dialogue, and Ben Burtt, the sound designer, created WALL-E's voice.
Films set largely in space or on another.Passengers: A malfunction wakes a man from hibernation 90 years early on a spaceship.
Films set largely in space or on another.Ad Astra: Brad Pitt's 2019 film sends an astronaut to Neptune to find his missing father.
Films set largely in space or on another.Lightyear: A 2022 Pixar film shown as the movie that inspired the Buzz Lightyear toy in the Toy Story world.
Films set largely in space or on another.Treasure Planet: Disney's 2002 sci-fi retelling of Treasure Island was an expensive box-office flop.
Films set largely in space or on another.Avatar: It takes place on Pandora, a moon orbiting a gas giant in Alpha Centauri, and became the highest-grossing film ever.
Films set largely in space or on another.Dune: It's set on the desert planet Arrakis. Villeneuve filmed the 2021 version in Jordan and Abu Dhabi.
Films set largely in space or on another.Star Wars: Every film begins with A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, so the planets are not Earth.
Films set largely in space or on another.Jaws: Set on the sea and the beaches of Amity Island, entirely on Earth. The mechanical shark, nicknamed Bruce, kept failing during filming.
Films set largely in space or on another.Titanic: The ship sinks in the North Atlantic, so the setting is Earth's ocean.
Films set largely in space or on another.The Abyss: Underwater aliens, but the film is set in a deep-sea oil rig, not space.
Films set largely in space or on another.Twister: Set among Oklahoma storm chasers, firmly on Earth.
Films set largely in space or on another.Inception: Takes place inside dreams, not outer space.
An alien visits Earth and the story stays in California suburbs, so it isn't set on another planet.
Films set largely in space or on another.Arrival: Aliens land on Earth, and the story is set here, so it doesn't count.
Films set largely in space or on another.Signs: Crop circles in rural Pennsylvania, so the aliens come to Earth.
Films set largely in space or on another.Men in Black: Set in New York, where aliens secretly live among us.
Films set largely in space or on another.Jurassic Park: Takes place on a fictional island near Costa Rica, so it's Earth.
Films set largely in space or on another.Finding Nemo: The story takes place in the ocean, not space.
Films set largely in space or on another.Waterworld: A flooded future Earth, not another planet.

Sitcom dads.Homer Simpson: The Simpsons' dad was named after creator Matt Groening's own father, Homer, and the show has run since 1989.
Sitcom dads.Peter Griffin: Seth MacFarlane has said Peter's voice came from a security guard at his college, and he also voices Stewie, Brian and Quagmire.
Sitcom dads.Phil Dunphy: Modern Family's dad, played by Ty Burrell, calls himself a 'cool dad' and is known for his goofy catchphrases and magic tricks.
Sitcom dads.Danny Tanner: The neat-freak widower of Full House, played by Bob Saget, who is also known for his stand-up comedy.
Sitcom dads.Al Bundy: The shoe salesman of Married... with Children, who famously reminisces about scoring four touchdowns in a single game at Polk High.
Sitcom dads.Tim Taylor: Tim Allen's 'Tool Man' of Home Improvement grunts at power tools, and his show-within-a-show is Tool Time.
Sitcom dads.Ray Barone: Everybody Loves Raymond drew on Ray Romano's own life, and Ray's envied brother Robert was inspired by Romano's real brother, a cop.
Sitcom dads.Hank Hill: King of the Hill's propane salesman in Arlen, Texas, was voiced by Mike Judge, who also created Beavis and Butt-Head.
Sitcom dads.Bob Belcher: The burger-flipping father in Bob's Burgers is voiced by H. Jon Benjamin, who also voices Archer.
Sitcom dads.Carl Winslow: Reggie VelJohnson played the Chicago cop dad on Family Matters, the household of the unstoppable Steve Urkel.
Sitcom dads.Mike Brady: The architect dad of The Brady Bunch had three sons, and the cast of six kids was famously arranged in a grid for the opening titles.
Sitcom dads.Bandit: Bluey's dad is a blue heeler who plays endless imaginative games. Bandit is a dog, but he's a classic sitcom-style father figure.
Sitcom dads.Red Forman: The gruff father in That '70s Show, played by Kurtwood Smith, is known for threatening to put his foot in someone's behind.
Sitcom dads.Marge Simpson: Matt Groening named her after his mother Margaret, and her towering blue beehive hairdo is one of TV's most recognizable.
Sitcom dads.Lois Griffin: The Family Guy mom is voiced by Alex Borstein, who also voices Tricia Takanawa and won Emmys for The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel.
Sitcom dads.Claire Dunphy: The Modern Family mom, played by Julie Bowen, who won two Emmys for the role. She is a mother, not a dad.
Sitcom dads.Peggy Bundy: The big-haired, lazy wife in Married... with Children is played by Katey Sagal, who later starred in Sons of Anarchy.
Sitcom dads.Debra Barone: Patricia Heaton's character on Everybody Loves Raymond has her patience tested by Ray and his meddling parents, who live across the street.
Sitcom dads.Peggy Hill: Hank's wife in King of the Hill is a substitute teacher who believes she is fluent in Spanish. She's not a dad, however.
Sitcom dads.Linda Belcher: Bob's endlessly cheerful wife is voiced by a man, comedian John Roberts, who also plays Linda's sister.
Sitcom dads.Carol Brady: The Brady Bunch mom, played by Florence Henderson, a mother of three girls who marries a man with three sons.
Sitcom dads.Chilli: Bluey's mom is a red heeler, a mother and not a dad, who works in airport security.
Sitcom dads.Kitty Forman: Red's wife on That '70s Show is played by Debra Jo Rupp, who is known for her loud and distinctive cackle.
Sitcom dads.Lorelai Gilmore: Lauren Graham plays the fast-talking mother in Gilmore Girls, which started in 2000 and is a mom-and-daughter show, not a dad-centered one.

Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Aida: It premiered in Cairo in 1871, and its Triumphal March is among opera's most famous scenes.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.La Traviata: Based on Dumas fils's novel The Lady of the Camellias, the title means the fallen woman or the one who strayed.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Rigoletto: Verdi kept La donna è mobile secret until the premiere so nobody could whistle it beforehand.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Otello: Verdi came out of semi-retirement for this 1887 Shakespeare adaptation, a gap of sixteen years after Aida.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Falstaff: His last opera, a comedy, written when he was nearly 80, in 1893, from Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Nabucco: The chorus Va, pensiero from this 1842 hit became an unofficial anthem of Italian unity.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Il Trovatore: Its Anvil Chorus sounds like workers hammering in rhythm. It's one of Verdi's most popular tunes.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Macbeth: His first Shakespeare opera, from 1847, with a famous sleepwalking scene for Lady Macbeth.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Don Carlos: Based on Schiller's play and written for the Paris Opéra, it's one of Verdi's longest works.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.La Bohème: Puccini's tale of poor Parisian artists, and not Verdi's, which later inspired the musical Rent.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Tosca: Puccini's, not Verdi's, and it ends with the heroine leaping from Rome's Castel Sant'Angelo.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Madama Butterfly: Puccini's story set in Nagasaki, not Verdi's, and the musical Miss Saigon retells it in Vietnam.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Carmen: Bizet's French opera from 1875, not Verdi's, and one of the most performed operas in the world.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.The Magic Flute: Mozart's last-year masterpiece, so not Verdi's, with the Queen of the Night's very high aria.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Don Giovanni: Mozart's, not Verdi's, and a trap next to Verdi's Don Carlos, as both share a Spanish title hero.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Barber of Seville: Rossini's comic opera of 1816, a Figaro tale with a famous overture, so not by Verdi.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Turandot: Puccini's last opera, left unfinished at his death, and it contains Nessun dorma. Not by Verdi.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Fidelio: Beethoven's only opera, which he reworked many times, and not Verdi's.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Lohengrin: Wagner's, not Verdi's, and its Bridal Chorus is the traditional Here Comes the Bride.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Norma: Bellini's, not Verdi's, with the soprano aria Casta diva, among the most famous in opera.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Pagliacci: Leoncavallo's 1892 tale of a clown, often paired in a double bill with Mascagni's Cavalleria rusticana.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Lucia di Lammermoor: Donizetti's, not Verdi's, and famous for the soprano's harrowing mad scene.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Tannhäuser: Wagner's, not Verdi's, and a medieval singing contest drives its plot.
Operas by Giuseppe Verdi.Eugene Onegin: Tchaikovsky's opera from Pushkin's verse novel, so Russian and not Verdi's.

Things that play music.Jukebox: Coin-operated jukeboxes date to the 1890s. In their 1940s heyday, Wurlitzer made them glow with color and bubbling tubes.
Things that play music.Gramophone: Emile Berliner patented the flat-disc gramophone in 1887. Its horn amplified sound with no electricity at all.
Things that play music.iPod: Apple's first iPod in 2001 promised a thousand songs in your pocket. It sold over 400 million units before the iPhone absorbed its role.
Things that play music.Walkman: Sony's 1979 Walkman nearly got a different name in the US, where it was sold as the Soundabout. The Walkman name later won out worldwide.
Things that play music.Boombox: The bulky stereo cassette players of the 1980s became symbols of hip hop and street culture, and some models ate up a lot of D batteries.
Things that play music.Music box: A rotating pinned cylinder plucks the tuned steel teeth of a comb to make notes. Swiss makers perfected the mechanism in the 1800s.
Things that play music.Radio: The first AM music broadcasts happened in the early 1900s. Marconi's wireless work in the 1890s laid the groundwork.
Things that play music.Turntable: Direct-drive turntables, popular with DJs, became standard after the Technics SL-1200 arrived in 1972. DJs also use them as instruments for scratching.
Things that play music.Smart speaker: Amazon's Echo launched in 2014. Voice assistants like Alexa can play music on request, which is the main thing people use them for.
Things that play music.Car stereo: The first car radio was sold by Motorola in 1930. Today's cars may offer AM, FM, satellite and streaming together.
Things that play music.Player piano: These pianos used punched paper rolls to play themselves. Composers like Stravinsky and Nancarrow wrote music just for them.
Things that play music.Ice cream truck: The jingle played by many US trucks is often Turkey in the Straw or Greensleeves. Chimes started as a way to avoid shouting.
Things that play music.Microwave: It beeps but does not play music. Raytheon's Percy Spencer discovered microwave heating when a candy bar melted in his pocket.
Things that play music.Toaster: The pop-up toaster was invented in 1919. Early versions could only brown one side of the bread at a time.
Things that play music.Fax machine: It sends printed pages down phone lines. It can make screeching noises but not music, though the modem sounds are a kind of language.
Things that play music.Calculator: Basic calculators don't play music. The first handheld, Texas Instruments's Cal Tech in 1967, was a bulky prototype.
Things that play music.Typewriter: It clatters but does not play music. The QWERTY layout was meant to reduce jams by separating common letter pairs.
Things that play music.Sundial: A sundial tells time only when the sun shines. The oldest examples date back to ancient Egypt.
Things that play music.Lamp: Lamps make light, not music. Edison's 1879 bulb famously glowed for about 13 hours in its first test before improved filaments lasted far longer.
Things that play music.Stapler: A stapler binds paper and plays nothing. The classic desk model is so standard that Swingline's red version starred in the film Office Space.
Things that play music.Kettle: A whistling kettle makes one note, but it is a signal, not a player of music. Electric kettles first appeared in the 1890s.
Things that play music.Telescope: A telescope magnifies distant objects and does not play music. Galileo's 1609 versions magnified only about three times.
Things that play music.Abacus: The abacus is a counting frame that has been in use for thousands of years. It clicks, but it does not play tunes.
Things that play music.Compass: A compass points north using magnetism and doesn't play a thing. Chinese sailors used magnetic compasses by about the 11th century.

Wrestling moves.Full nelson: The full nelson locks both arms behind the head from behind, forcing the neck forward. It's a classic hold that is illegal in amateur folkstyle wrestling.
Wrestling moves.Half nelson: The half nelson passes one arm under the opponent's arm, and it's a staple in amateur wrestling to turn opponents onto their back.
Wrestling moves.Suplex: A suplex throws an opponent backwards over the attacker's body, and it was brought to fame by Karl Gotch.
Wrestling moves.Piledriver: The piledriver drops an opponent headfirst, and it is banned in many promotions because it's dangerous.
Wrestling moves.Headlock: The headlock traps the head under one's arm, one of the oldest wrestling holds, and it is often used as a rest hold.
Wrestling moves.Body slam: The body slam lifts an opponent and throws them flat on their back, a staple that was made famous by Hulk Hogan against Andre the Giant.
Wrestling moves.Takedown: In amateur wrestling a takedown brings an opponent to the mat and scores points, often by shooting for the legs.
Wrestling moves.Dropkick: A dropkick is leaping and kicking with both feet, and is seen as a high-flying move in pro wrestling.
Wrestling moves.Chokeslam: A chokeslam grabs the opponent's throat and slams them down, and it was famously associated with The Undertaker and Kane.
Wrestling moves.Clothesline: A clothesline is an outstretched arm strike to the neck or chest, with a name borrowed from the hanging laundry line.
Wrestling moves.Figure four: The figure four leglock was popularized by Ric Flair, and it gets its name because the legs form a number 4.
Wrestling moves.DDT: The DDT, a name credited to Jake Roberts, drops an opponent on their head, and it's said to be named after the pesticide.
Wrestling moves.Ollie: An ollie is a skateboard jump, where the board pops up without the hands.
Wrestling moves.Kickflip: A kickflip is a skateboard trick where the board flips under your feet.
Wrestling moves.Lutz: A lutz is a figure skating jump with a toe pick, named after Alois Lutz.
Wrestling moves.Axel: An axel is a figure skating jump, named after Axel Paulsen, and it has an extra half rotation.
Wrestling moves.Jab: A jab is a quick straight punch in boxing.
Wrestling moves.Slam dunk: A slam dunk is a basketball move, which uses a similar word but isn't a wrestling move.
Wrestling moves.Lob: A lob is a high looping shot in tennis or soccer.
Wrestling moves.Fosbury flop: The Fosbury flop is a high jump technique.
Wrestling moves.Hail Mary: A Hail Mary is a long desperate pass in football.
Wrestling moves.Googly: A googly is a cricket delivery that spins the opposite way, confusing batters.
Wrestling moves.Nutmeg: A nutmeg is a soccer trick of passing through an opponent's legs.
Wrestling moves.Volley: A volley is a tennis or soccer shot hit before the ball bounces.

Word games.Scrabble: Architect Alfred Butts made it in the Depression and counted letters in The New York Times to set tile values. It began as Criss-Crosses.
Word games.Boggle: Players hunt words in a shaken 4x4 grid of letter cubes against a three-minute timer. It dates from 1972.
Word games.Bananagrams: Its letter tiles arrive in a banana-shaped pouch. Abraham Nathanson and family created it in 2006, and everyone races to build grids at once.
Word games.Wordle: Josh Wardle first made it for his partner. The New York Times bought it in early 2022 for a reported price in the low seven figures.
Word games.Hangman: A guessing game that has been played since at least the Victorian era. Starting with common letters like E and T is the classic opening.
Word games.Words with Friends: Launched in 2009 as an asynchronous mobile Scrabble rival. Zynga bought its developer Newtoy in 2010.
Word games.Taboo: Describe a word without saying it or five forbidden clues, with a buzzer to punish slips. Hasbro published it in 1989.
Word games.Codenames: Two spymasters give one-word clues to link words on a grid of 25. It won the 2016 Spiel des Jahres, and Vlaada Chvatil designed it.
Word games.Scattergories: Players list items in categories starting with a given letter, but any answer two players share gets cancelled. So obscure beats obvious.
Word games.Upwords: Like Scrabble, but letters can be stacked on top of existing tiles to make new words. Milton Bradley released it in 1981.
Word games.Crossword: The New York Times resisted running one until 1942, long calling the puzzles a waste of time, and now has a famous daily crossword.
Word games.Spelling Bee: Made famous by the New York Times's daily puzzle. The national contest in the US has run since 1925.
Word games.Sudoku: A numbers puzzle: fill a grid with 1 to 9 without repeats. It looks like a word puzzle but never touches a letter.
Word games.Chess: Chess is about strategy on 64 squares. The number of possible games vastly exceeds the atoms in the universe, but no letters are involved.
Word games.Connect Four: A vertical grid where you drop discs to line up four. It was solved in 1988: the first player wins with perfect play. No words.
Word games.Yahtzee: A dice game whose name echoes yacht: Edwin Lowe reportedly bought the rights from a couple playing it on their boat. Numbers, not letters.
Word games.Monopoly: Derived from Lizzie Magie's 1904 Landlord's Game, which was meant to show the harm of monopolies. Money, not words.
Word games.Risk: Strategy conquest game made by French film director Albert Lamorisse in 1957. It's armies and dice.
Word games.Jenga: Wooden blocks stacked into a wobbly tower. Its name is Swahili for to build, and it tests steady hands.
Word games.Battleship: Began as a pencil-and-paper guessing game long before Milton Bradley's 1967 plastic edition. Coordinates, not words.
Word games.Minesweeper: Windows 3.1 included it in 1992, teaching a generation to click. It uses number logic, not word skills.
Word games.Tetris: Alexey Pajitnov made it in 1984 in the Soviet Union. Its tetromino pieces are shapes, not letters.
Word games.Kakuro: A number crossword in which digit runs must add to clues. It looks like a word puzzle but uses numbers.
Word games.Mastermind: A code-breaking game with coloured pegs, invented by Mordecai Meirowitz in 1970. Colours, not letters.

LEGO themes.Star Wars: Began in 1999 as LEGO's first licensed theme. The giant UCS Millennium Falcon set has over 7,500 pieces.
LEGO themes.City: Launched in 2005, replacing the older Town theme. It features fire stations, police and airports.
LEGO themes.Technic: Began in 1977 as Expert Builder, adding gears, motors and pneumatics to the brick.
LEGO themes.Ninjago: Launched in 2011 with spinjitzu and grew into a TV series and a 2017 movie.
LEGO themes.Friends: Launched in 2012 around five friends in Heartlake City, aimed at girls and a huge hit.
LEGO themes.Duplo: Bricks twice the size, introduced in 1969 so toddlers can't swallow them, yet they still fit regular bricks.
LEGO themes.Creator: Each set's pieces can be built into three different models, hence the 3-in-1 label.
LEGO themes.Harry Potter: Launched in 2001 to tie in with the first film. Hogwarts has been rebuilt in many sizes.
LEGO themes.Bionicle: Launched in 2001 with its own story of robot warriors. It ended in 2010, then briefly returned in 2015.
LEGO themes.Minecraft: Started from a fan-submitted idea in 2011 on the LEGO Ideas platform.
LEGO themes.Architecture: Landmark models launched in 2008, an idea from architect Adam Reed Tucker.
LEGO themes.Speed Champions: Mini versions of real cars from Ferrari, Porsche and others, launched in 2015.
LEGO themes.K'Nex: A rival built from rods and connectors, invented in 1992 by Joel Glickman.
LEGO themes.Playmobil: A German figure toy from 1974, conceived in an oil crisis plastic shortage by Hans Beck.
LEGO themes.Mega Bloks: A Canadian rival whose bricks fit LEGO's, now owned by Mattel since 2014.
LEGO themes.Lincoln Logs: A wooden log toy invented in 1916 by John Lloyd Wright, Frank Lloyd Wright's son.
LEGO themes.Meccano: Metal strips with nuts and bolts, invented in 1898 by Frank Hornby in Liverpool.
LEGO themes.Tinkertoy: Wooden spools and sticks, invented in 1914 by Charles Pajeau, a stonemason.
LEGO themes.Barbie: Mattel's doll from 1959, named after Ruth Handler's daughter Barbara.
LEGO themes.Polly Pocket: A tiny playset created for its inventor's daughter. It's a Mattel brand now.
LEGO themes.Nerf: Foam toys launched by Parker Brothers in 1969, now Hasbro's.
LEGO themes.Magna-Tiles: Magnetic building tiles for 3D shapes, not a LEGO line.
LEGO themes.Erector Set: A metal construction kit launched in 1913 by A.C. Gilbert.

Ways to go fishing.Fly fishing: The angler casts a nearly weightless artificial fly with the line's weight carrying it. Hand-tied flies imitate insects fish eat.
Ways to go fishing.Ice fishing: Anglers drill holes through frozen lakes, sometimes on ice thick enough to drive on, and some set up tiny heated shacks.
Ways to go fishing.Spearfishing: Practiced for millennia, spearfishing today is often done freediving with a spear gun, holding breath at depth.
Ways to go fishing.Deep sea fishing: Deep sea anglers head far offshore after big game like marlin and tuna, with fish that can top 1,000 pounds.
Ways to go fishing.Trolling: Trolling means dragging lures or baited lines behind a moving boat. The same word describes internet provocation, but that's a separate meaning.
Ways to go fishing.Noodling: Noodlers catch catfish with bare hands by sticking an arm in an underwater hole. It's legal in only some US states.
Ways to go fishing.Surf fishing: Anglers cast from a beach into breaking waves, often long rods, targeting fish like striped bass and redfish.
Ways to go fishing.Bowfishing: Bowfishing uses a bow and a line-attached arrow to shoot fish near the surface, often at night under lights.
Ways to go fishing.Jigging: Jigging works a weighted, brightly colored lure up and down to draw strikes, and it works through ice or in deep water.
Ways to go fishing.Carp fishing: Carp fishing is a serious pursuit in Europe, with anglers using bait and rigs for fish that can reach 30 kilos.
Ways to go fishing.Kayak fishing: Anglers fish from kayaks, which let them reach shallow spots and sometimes go out beyond the surf.
Ways to go fishing.Phishing: Phishing is online fraud in which scammers try to steal passwords, and the 'ph' spelling echoes phone hacking of the 1990s. It sounds like fishing but is a trap.
Ways to go fishing.Whaling: Whaling means hunting whales, not fishing, since whales are mammals. Commercial whaling was banned by the IWC in 1986.
Ways to go fishing.Snorkeling: Snorkelers watch fish rather than catch them. Maybe the closest to fishing is looking.
Ways to go fishing.Birdwatching: Birdwatching targets birds, not fish, and it's one of the most popular nature hobbies.
Ways to go fishing.Ice skating: Ice skaters glide on frozen lakes, but they don't fish. Though ice fishing shares the same frozen setting.
Ways to go fishing.Stargazing: Stargazing looks at the night sky; no catching involved, unless you count the bragging rights.
Ways to go fishing.Beachcombing: Beachcombers search shores for shells and driftwood, and sea glass is often collected.
Ways to go fishing.Rafting: Rafters ride rapids in an inflatable boat, and the thrill comes from whitewater, not fish.
Ways to go fishing.Wakeboarding: Wakeboarders are towed over a boat's wake on a short board, and the sport grew from water skiing and surfing.
Ways to go fishing.Sailing: Sailing moves a boat with wind. Fishing and sailing can combine, but sailing itself isn't a fishing method.
Ways to go fishing.Spelunking: Spelunking is the American term for recreational caving, nothing to do with fishing.
Ways to go fishing.Surfing: Surfers ride waves, and the 'surf' in surf fishing refers only to the breaking water.
Ways to go fishing.Bobsledding: Bobsledders race down an icy track in a sled, at speeds over 130 km/h.

The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Nemean Lion: A beast with a hide no weapon could pierce, so Heracles strangled it. He then wore its skin as a cloak, the first labor.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Lernaean Hydra: A multi-headed serpent whose heads regrew when severed. Heracles had his nephew burn each stump to stop it.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Erymanthian Boar: A huge boar Heracles had to bring back alive. He chased it into deep snow and trapped it.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Augean stables: Heracles cleaned them in a day by redirecting two rivers through them. Today the phrase means a huge mess to clean.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Stymphalian birds: Man-eating birds with metal feathers. Heracles frightened them with a bronze rattle and shot them as they fled.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Cretan Bull: A great bull from Crete that Heracles captured and carried to Eurystheus. It was the father of the Minotaur in some stories.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Cerynitian Hind: A golden-horned deer sacred to Artemis. Heracles chased it for a year to take it alive.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Mares of Diomedes: Man-eating horses of the Thracian king Diomedes. Heracles fed the king to his own mares.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Girdle of Hippolyta: The belt of the Amazon queen, given to her by Ares. The ninth labor ended in a fight, not a gift.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Cattle of Geryon: The red cattle of a three-bodied giant, whom Heracles killed at the far west of the world. The tenth labor.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Golden apples: Taken from the garden of the Hesperides. Heracles either tricked Atlas into fetching them or picked them himself.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Cerberus: The three-headed hound of Hades, fetched as the final and hardest labor. Heracles carried him up alive without weapons.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Minotaur: A trap: it was killed by Theseus, not Heracles. It doesn't appear in the twelve labors.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Medusa: Perseus beheaded her. She is not one of the twelve labors.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Chimera: A fire-breathing hybrid killed by Bellerophon, not Heracles, who never faced it.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Golden Fleece: The prize of Jason and the Argonauts. Heracles started on that voyage but left early.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Cyclops: One-eyed giants met by Odysseus. Heracles' labors didn't include them.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Sphinx: The riddling monster of Thebes that Oedipus defeated. It isn't a labor of Heracles.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Python: The giant serpent slain by Apollo at Delphi. Another beast, not on Heracles' list.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Kraken: A trap: it's a Norse sea monster, not from Greek myth at all.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Pegasus: Bellerophon's winged horse, never one of the twelve labors.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Trojan Horse: Odysseus's trick to end the Trojan War. Heracles did sack Troy once earlier, but the horse is another story.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Scylla: A sea monster Odysseus faced on his voyage home. Not one of Heracles' labors.
The Twelve Labors of Heracles.Calydonian Boar: A giant boar sent by Artemis and hunted by a band of heroes, including Atalanta. It's different from the Erymanthian Boar.

Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Golden mask: The famous burial mask is about 11 kg of solid gold inlaid with lapis lazuli and glass. Its shoulders carry a magical spell to protect the king.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Chariots: Six dismantled chariots were found, some plated in gold. Tutankhamun was likely not a warrior king, yet he was buried with the means to ride into battle.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Canopic jars: These held the king's preserved liver, lungs, stomach and intestines. Tut's were carved in a single block of calcite, in an alabaster chest.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Golden throne: Covered in gold and silver and inlaid with glass and stone, its backrest shows the young king and his queen Ankhesenamun. It is the finest piece of Egyptian furniture known.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Senet board: Senet was a board game popular for thousands of years, and four boards were buried with Tut so he could play in the afterlife. Its exact rules are now lost.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Sandals: Over 90 pairs of footwear were found. One pair had enemies drawn on the soles so the king would trample them with each step.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Iron dagger: A rare iron blade, made when iron was scarcer than gold. Analysis shows the metal was from a meteorite, a gift that fell from the sky.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Shabti figures: More than 400 small statues were meant to work in the afterlife in Tut's place, so he would not have to do farm labour himself.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Model boats: Around 35 model boats were packed in for the king's journeys to the next world, including sailing on the Nile and visiting sacred sites.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Trumpets: Two trumpets, one silver and one bronze or copper, were found. One was played in a BBC radio broadcast in 1939, a reported 150 million people tuned in.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Sarcophagus: Tut lay in three nested coffins inside a stone sarcophagus. The innermost was solid gold, and weighed about 110 kg.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Beds: Funerary beds in animal shapes, such as a cow and a lion, were found. The pieces were ritual couches for the king's journey after death.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Rosetta Stone: Found in 1799 by French soldiers, long after Tut's time. It dates to 196 BC, roughly 1,100 years after the pharaoh died.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Coins: Egypt used no coins when Tut ruled around 1330 BC. Coinage was invented some 700 years later, in Lydia. Trade used goods and weighed metal.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Potatoes: A New World crop, unknown outside the Andes until after the 1500s. No Egyptian would have eaten one.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Paper books: Egyptians wrote on papyrus scrolls, and bound books arrived much later. Tut's tomb has inscriptions and spells, but no codex.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Gunpowder: A Chinese invention from about the 9th century AD, over two thousand years after Tut. It could not have been in his tomb.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Eyeglasses: They first appeared in Italy in the 1280s, some 2,600 years later. Egyptians relied on eyes alone, with kohl against the glare.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Coffee: Coffee drinking began in Ethiopia or Yemen, and no sign of it exists in ancient Egypt. Its use as a drink was medieval.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Tomatoes: Another New World plant, brought to Europe only after Columbus. Tut never saw a tomato.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Horseshoes: Not used in Egypt then. Horses pulled chariots unshod, and nailed-on iron horseshoes came to Europe about 2,000 years later.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Playing cards: Cards arrived in Europe in the 1300s, likely from the Islamic world. Tut's gaming was with senet board and dice.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Chess set: Chess evolved in India around the 6th century AD, almost two thousand years after Tut's burial. His board game was senet.
Found in Tutankhamun's tomb.Compass: The magnetic compass came from China about a thousand years ago, far too late for Tut. Egyptians navigated by the Nile and the stars.

Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Great Pyramid: Built around 2560 BC, it was already ancient when Cleopatra lived nearer in time to the Moon landing than to its building.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Sphinx: Carved from a single limestone outcrop, it was already over 2,000 years old in her day, and drifting sand often buried it.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Parthenon: Finished in 432 BC, it was about four centuries old by her time and stood in a Greece then ruled by Rome.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Stonehenge: Raised around 2500 BC, its main stones were already some 2,500 years old and long abandoned in her day.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Great Library: Founded by her Ptolemaic ancestors in Alexandria, it stood in her own capital, and part of it burned during Caesar's war there.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Pharos of Alexandria: This lighthouse of Alexandria rose around 280 BC in her capital and kept working for centuries after her death.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Olympic Games: Tradition dates the first Games to 776 BC, so they were over 700 years old when Cleopatra was born.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Papyrus: Egyptians had written on this reed-based paper for nearly 3,000 years before her; their monopoly made it a prized export.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Coins: Invented in Lydia around 600 BC, they were old news; Cleopatra even issued her own coins bearing her portrait.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Rome: Founded, by tradition, in 753 BC, it was already a Mediterranean superpower, and both Caesar and Antony were its leaders.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Colosseum: Opened in AD 80, it appeared about 110 years after Cleopatra's death in 30 BC.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Taj Mahal: Shah Jahan built it in the 1600s, roughly 1,700 years after she died, as a tomb for his wife.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Machu Picchu: The Inca built it around 1450, some 1,500 years after Cleopatra's death, and no Roman or Egyptian ever heard of it.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Hagia Sophia: The current building was completed in AD 537 under Justinian, more than five centuries after she lived.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Printing press: Gutenberg's European press arrived around 1450, nearly 1,500 years after her death, so her library was copied by hand.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Hadrian's Wall: Begun in AD 122 under Emperor Hadrian, more than 150 years after Cleopatra died.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Notre-Dame: Work began in 1163, over 1,100 years after her death, on an island in the Seine.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Tower of London: William the Conqueror started the White Tower in the 1070s, about 11 centuries after she died.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Gunpowder: Chinese alchemists stumbled on it around the 9th century AD, nearly 900 years after her death.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Eyeglasses: Italian craftsmen made the first ones around the 1280s, some 1,300 years after Cleopatra died, so she never wore a pair.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Angkor Wat: Built in the early 1100s as a Hindu temple for Suryavarman II, it came more than a thousand years after her death.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Chichen Itza: Its great pyramid-temple rose many centuries after Cleopatra's death, so neither she nor Rome knew of the Maya.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Big Ben: The bell was cast in 1858, and Cleopatra died nearly 1,900 years before it first rang.
Already existed when Cleopatra was alive.Tower of Pisa: Construction began in 1173, and the famous tilt started early because the tower was built on soft ground.

Cleaning products.Bleach: Never mix bleach with ammonia or acidic cleaners; the combination releases toxic gases such as chloramine or chlorine.
Cleaning products.Dish soap: Wildlife rescuers use plain dish soap to clean oil-coated seabirds, since it breaks the grease's grip on feathers.
Cleaning products.Window cleaner: Many sprays contain ammonia or alcohol so they evaporate fast without streaks, and newspaper became a classic lint-free polishing cloth.
Cleaning products.Furniture polish: A polish leaves a thin film of wax or oil that fills tiny scratches, which is why dull wood looks richer after a wipe.
Cleaning products.Laundry detergent: Modern detergents replaced soap partly because they don't form scum in hard water, using synthetic cleaning molecules called surfactants.
Cleaning products.Oven cleaner: Many are strongly alkaline, often built on sodium hydroxide (lye), which turns baked-on grease into soap that wipes away.
Cleaning products.Toilet cleaner: Many are mildly acidic, designed to dissolve limescale that ordinary soap can't touch.
Cleaning products.Disinfectant wipes: For the wipe to actually kill germs, the surface usually has to stay visibly wet for the label's contact time, often a few minutes.
Cleaning products.Scouring powder: The gritty part is usually a fine mineral such as calcium carbonate, hard enough to scrub but soft enough not to gouge most porcelain.
Cleaning products.Stain remover: Many rely on enzymes, proteins that chew up other proteins, fats or starches, so the right remover depends on the stain.
Cleaning products.Floor cleaner: Floor cleaners are formulated to leave little residue, since leftover film can feel sticky and attract fresh dirt.
Cleaning products.Mayonnaise: It's food, not cleaner, though home-hackers do use it on sticker residue; its real fame is the sandwich.
Cleaning products.Olive oil: Food, not cleaner; Mediterranean cooks have used it for thousands of years, and ancient Greek athletes rubbed it on their skin.
Cleaning products.Hairspray: Personal care, not cleaning; people sometimes use it as a folk remedy to lift ink, which is why it can seem to belong.
Cleaning products.Sunscreen: A skincare product; SPF measures how much longer skin takes to redden than bare skin, mainly against UVB rays.
Cleaning products.Perfume: Eau de parfum typically holds about 15 to 20 percent fragrance oil in alcohol, so it's a cosmetic, not a cleaner.
Cleaning products.Glue: A craft and repair adhesive; ancient Egyptians already used animal-hide glues thousands of years ago.
Cleaning products.Paint: A coating, the opposite of a cleaner; paint is pigment, binder and solvent, and ochre-based paints are tens of thousands of years old.
Cleaning products.Ketchup: It really does clean: ketchup's mild acid dissolves the dull oxide layer on tarnished copper pans, though it's still a condiment.
Cleaning products.Lip balm: Personal care; beeswax and petrolatum are common ingredients that seal in moisture rather than add it.
Cleaning products.Moisturizer: Skincare, not cleaning; many contain humectants such as glycerin that draw water into the skin's top layer.
Cleaning products.Nail polish: A cosmetic lacquer, though a dab of clear polish is a known trick to seal a loose screw or stop a shoelace tip from fraying.
Cleaning products.Cough syrup: Medicine, not cleaner; the thick syrup base mostly coats the throat, which is part of why it soothes.
Cleaning products.Vanilla extract: A baking ingredient made by steeping vanilla beans in alcohol; vanilla is often called the second most expensive spice after saffron.

Tools used to measure something.Ruler: The ruler's ancestors include 4,500-year-old Indus Valley rods; 'ruler' also means king since both 'rule' lines or lands.
Tools used to measure something.Tape measure: A tape measure's curved steel blade stands stiff across a gap, using the same arch principle as a pipe.
Tools used to measure something.Thermometer: Daniel Fahrenheit built the first reliable mercury thermometer in 1714.
Tools used to measure something.Bathroom scale: Most use strain gauges, strips of metal that change electrical resistance when slightly bent by your weight.
Tools used to measure something.Measuring cup: A US cup is about 237 milliliters, yet recipes in Australia use 250-milliliter cups.
Tools used to measure something.Stopwatch: Louis Moinet and Nicolas Rieussec built early chronographs; Rieussec's 1821 version marked horse races with ink dots.
Tools used to measure something.Protractor: Protractors divide a circle into 360 degrees, a legacy of Babylonian base-60 math.
