Tools used to measure something.Barometer: Torricelli built the first mercury barometer in 1643; falling pressure often signals stormy weather.
Tools used to measure something.Speedometer: Croatian inventor Josip Belušić presented a 'velocimeter' in 1888, an early speedometer.
Tools used to measure something.Measuring spoon: A US tablespoon is 15 milliliters but an Australian one is 20, a trap for bakers.
Tools used to measure something.Rain gauge: One millimeter of rain equals one liter of water per square meter of ground.
Tools used to measure something.Odometer: The Roman engineer Vitruvius described a cart odometer that dropped a pebble every mile.
Tools used to measure something.Hammer: It strikes, not measures; a doctor's reflex hammer tests nerve response, not quantity.
Tools used to measure something.Funnel: It guides liquids into narrow openings, but has no markings, so it measures nothing.
Tools used to measure something.Whisk: A whisk mixes, and whipping egg whites in a copper bowl helps stabilize them.
Tools used to measure something.Stapler: It fastens; the common staple size 26/6 describes the wire gauge and leg length.
Tools used to measure something.Scissors: It cuts, not measures; the pivoting two-blade design is more than 3,000 years old.
Tools used to measure something.Paintbrush: Paintbrushes appear in prehistoric cave art, but they apply color rather than gauge anything.
Tools used to measure something.Sponge: A natural sponge soaks up water but gauges nothing; it is an animal that filters water through its body.
Tools used to measure something.Pliers: It grips and bends, though some multi-tool pliers have a ruler etched into the handle.
Tools used to measure something.Ladle: A standard ladle isn't marked, though restaurants buy portion-control ladles with set volumes.
Tools used to measure something.Broom: Brooms sweep; the old 'besom' of bundled twigs is the traditional style.
Tools used to measure something.Eraser: Before rubber erasers, bread crumbs were used to rub out pencil, until Joseph Priestley noted rubber's talent in 1770.
Tools used to measure something.Colander: It drains pasta; its holes release water rather than meter volume.

Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Lego brick: Lego bricks are molded to tolerances of a few thousandths of a millimeter, tough enough that one underfoot hurts, and they rarely break.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Thumbtack: The thumbtack always lands point up in cartoons, but in real life the flat head often does too, since it weighs more.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Broken glass: Broken glass causes cuts that can be deep, and tiny shards can hide in carpet for years.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Pine cone: A pine cone has stiff woody scales, and it opens in dry weather to release its seeds.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Bee: A honeybee leaves its stinger and venom sac in your skin, and she dies soon after.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Toy jack: Jacks have six sharp points, which means one always faces up on a floor.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Sea urchin: Sea urchin spines can break off in your skin and are painful, and some species carry venom.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Nail: A rusty nail is a tetanus risk, so a puncture should be checked and your tetanus shot kept up to date.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Cactus: Cactus spines are modified leaves, which often come with tiny barbed hairs that are hard to pull out.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Bottle cap: A bottle cap has a crimped edge of 21 points, which is the standard for crown caps.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Stinging nettle: Nettles have tiny hollow hairs that inject histamine and other chemicals, causing hours of itch.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Hot coals: Coals can glow at over 1,000 degrees Fahrenheit, though firewalkers rely on the poor heat conductivity of ash.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Thistle: Thistles are the national emblem of Scotland, and legend says a Norse invader stepped on one and cried out.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Carpet: Carpet is soft and cushions your foot, which is why it is a barefoot favorite despite dust mites.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Grass: Grass is soft and cool, and walking barefoot on it, called grounding, is said by some to be relaxing.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Rug: A rug cushions the floor, and it is one of the easiest surfaces to cross barefoot.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Pillow: A pillow is soft and harmless underfoot, though it is certainly not meant to be stepped on.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Yoga mat: Yoga mats are designed to be barefoot surfaces, with a grippy texture that keeps feet from slipping.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Bath mat: A bath mat is for wet bare feet, and a rubber backing keeps it from slipping.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Towel: A towel is soft and safe underfoot, though a wet one on tile may be slippery.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Blanket: A blanket is soft and warm, and nothing sharp hides in it.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Moss: Moss is a soft carpet with no roots to catch your feet, and it has been used as a natural cushion for centuries.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Sock: A sock is a soft layer for your foot, and a lone sock on the floor is harmless, if irritating.
Things you'd regret stepping on barefoot.Slipper: Slippers are made for bare feet, so they are the one thing here that is safe to step into, and shearling ones keep toes toasty.

Things that soak up liquid.Sponge: Natural sea sponges are animals with no brain or organs, and a bath sponge is the dried skeleton of one.
Things that soak up liquid.Paper towel: Paper towels pull liquid in through tiny gaps between cellulose fibers, a effect called capillary action.
Things that soak up liquid.Bath towel: The cotton loops of terry cloth multiply surface area, which is why a fluffy towel drinks water far faster than a flat cloth.
Things that soak up liquid.Diaper: Modern diapers hold sodium polyacrylate crystals that can swallow many times their own weight in liquid and turn it to gel.
Things that soak up liquid.Cotton ball: Cotton fiber can hold roughly 25 times its own weight in water, which is why a small ball feels so thirsty.
Things that soak up liquid.Mop head: Microfiber mop heads are split into ultra-fine strands that trap far more liquid and grime than old cotton string heads.
Things that soak up liquid.Cat litter: Many litters are bentonite clay that clumps when wet, and the same stuff is spread on garage floors to soak up oil spills.
Things that soak up liquid.Sawdust: Sawdust was once strewn across tavern floors to catch spills, and workshops still use it to mop up oil and chemical leaks.
Things that soak up liquid.Blotting paper: Blotting paper dried fresh ink in the age of dip pens and fountain pens, and labs still use it to dry specimens.
Things that soak up liquid.Chamois: Real chamois leather came from a mountain antelope; today's car-wash chamois is usually oil-tanned sheepskin that holds lots of water.
Things that soak up liquid.Bread: Bread soaks up sauce so well that medieval diners ate from stale slabs of it called trenchers, then ate the plate.
Things that soak up liquid.Tissue: Tissue grabs liquid fast because its thin, loosely bonded fibers wick moisture through countless tiny gaps.
Things that soak up liquid.Plastic wrap: Cling film sticks by molecular attraction, but it is waterproof, so liquid beads up on it instead of soaking in.
Things that soak up liquid.Aluminum foil: Household foil is thinner than a human hair, yet it completely blocks water, light and oxygen.
Things that soak up liquid.Glass: Glass is nonporous, so it never absorbs flavors or liquids, which is why it is easy to sterilize and reuse.
Things that soak up liquid.Rubber glove: Most rubber gloves are natural latex, made from rubber tree sap, and form a waterproof barrier that liquid cannot enter.
Things that soak up liquid.Raincoat: Charles Macintosh patented waterproof fabric in 1823 by sandwiching rubber between cloth, and the mackintosh coat took his name.
Things that soak up liquid.Umbrella: Umbrellas began as sunshades thousands of years ago; making them rainproof came later, partly with oiled paper in China.
Things that soak up liquid.Wax paper: It looks like ordinary paper, but a wax coating seals the fibers, so liquid sits on top instead of soaking in.
Things that soak up liquid.Ceramic tile: Glazed tile is sealed by a glassy coating, which is exactly why bathrooms and kitchens use it for wet walls.
Things that soak up liquid.Mirror: A mirror is glass backed with a thin metal layer, often silver or aluminum, so liquid just runs off the surface.
Things that soak up liquid.Plastic bag: The one-piece plastic shopping bag was patented by a Swedish firm in the early 1960s and it is fully waterproof.
Things that soak up liquid.Steel pan: Carbon steel pans become naturally nonstick once seasoned with baked-on oil, a barrier that also repels water.
Things that soak up liquid.Rubber boot: Wellington boots are named for the Duke of Wellington, who asked for a trimmer leather boot; rubber versions came later.

Things usually made of leather.Belt: A good leather belt is made from the thick top layer of a cowhide, which is why it can last for decades.
Things usually made of leather.Wallet: Leather wallets soften and darken with use, developing a patina that many owners value.
Things usually made of leather.Baseball glove: Gloves are traditionally cowhide, and players rub in oil to soften them, a break-in ritual as old as the sport.
Things usually made of leather.Saddle: Saddles are made of leather because it is tough, flexible and molds to the rider and horse over many years.
Things usually made of leather.Briefcase: Leather briefcases date back centuries, and a classic one can be conditioned and passed down for generations.
Things usually made of leather.Cowboy boots: The tall shaft and angled heel of cowboy boots were designed for riding, keeping feet from slipping through stirrups.
Things usually made of leather.Biker jacket: The Schott Perfecto, first made in 1928, became legendary after Marlon Brando wore one in The Wild One in 1953.
Things usually made of leather.Bridle: A bridle is leather straps fitted around a horse's head, and good ones are stitched by saddlers by hand.
Things usually made of leather.Chesterfield sofa: The deep-buttoned leather Chesterfield is named after an Earl of Chesterfield, and its rolled arms are the same height as the back.
Things usually made of leather.T-shirt: T-shirts are typically jersey cotton, a soft knit that has nothing to do with animal hide.
Things usually made of leather.Bath towel: Bath towels are cotton terry, and thousands of loops help them absorb a lot of water.
Things usually made of leather.Wool scarf: Wool comes from sheep fleece, shorn without harming the animal, whereas leather comes from the hide.
Things usually made of leather.Rubber boots: Rubber boots come from rubber tree sap or synthetic rubber, which is waterproof in a way leather isn't.
Things usually made of leather.Silk tie: Silk comes from silkworm cocoons, and it takes hundreds of cocoons to make a single tie.
Things usually made of leather.Swimsuit: Swimsuits are usually nylon or polyester blended with spandex, chosen so they dry quickly and stretch.
Things usually made of leather.Raincoat: A raincoat is coated fabric or plastic, and leather would soak up water and stiffen.
Things usually made of leather.Plastic bag: The single-piece plastic bag was patented in the early 1960s, and leather has never been involved.
Things usually made of leather.Denim jeans: Many jeans have a small patch at the waistband that looks like leather, but is often a leather-like substitute.
Things usually made of leather.Paper bag: Paper bags are made from wood pulp, and the flat-bottomed grocery sack was invented in 1870s America.
Things usually made of leather.Bed sheet: Sheets are cotton, linen or similar fibers, and a leather sheet would be warm, heavy and hard to wash.
Things usually made of leather.Fleece: Many fleece jackets are made from recycled plastic bottles, a polyester fabric first branded Polartec in 1979.
Things usually made of leather.Tote bag: Tote bags are usually canvas or cotton, though a few designer ones are leather.
Things usually made of leather.Beanie: Beanies are knitted from wool or acrylic, since a stretchy hat needs fibers that can give.
Things usually made of leather.Puffer jacket: Eddie Bauer created the first quilted down jacket in 1936 after nearly dying of hypothermia on a fishing trip.

Things you'd find in a spice rack.Paprika: Paprika is ground dried peppers, and Hungary's version is so central to its cuisine that the country grades it by heat and sweetness.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Cumin: Cumin seeds have been found in ancient Egyptian tombs, and the spice gives chili and curry their earthy, warm flavor.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Oregano: Oregano's name comes from Greek words meaning 'joy of the mountain,' and it's the signature herb on pizza.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Cinnamon: Cinnamon is the inner bark of a tree; in ancient times it was so valuable that it was a gift fit for kings.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Turmeric: Turmeric gives curry its yellow color, and it's the plant's root, a close relative of ginger, that is ground to make it.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Nutmeg: Nutmeg comes from a seed, and its covering gives us a second spice, mace; in large doses nutmeg is actually toxic.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Dried basil: Basil is a member of the mint family, and the dried form is much more mellow than fresh basil in pesto.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Chili flakes: Chili flakes get their heat from capsaicin, which birds can't taste, so birds spread chili seeds without any burning.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Black pepper: Black pepper was once so valuable that it was used as currency, and it's the world's most traded spice.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Thyme: Thyme was used by ancient Egyptians in embalming, and its oil, thymol, is an ingredient in some mouthwashes.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Ground ginger: Ginger is a root, and the dried ground version is more pungent and hot, which makes it ideal for gingerbread.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Cloves: Cloves are dried flower buds, and for centuries they were so rare that they only grew on a few islands in Indonesia.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Flour: Flour is a pantry staple, not a spice, and a large bag may well be stored in a cabinet far from your spice rack.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Sugar: Sugar sweetens rather than seasons, and it lives in a canister since it is used by the cupful, not by the pinch.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Baking powder: Baking powder contains both an acid and a base so it makes bubbles when wet; it's a leavener, not a spice.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Cornstarch: Cornstarch thickens sauces, and it works at about twice the strength of flour, but it isn't a spice.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Rice: Rice is a staple grain, and more than half of the world depends on it, but it's too bulky for a spice rack.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Honey: Honey never spoils, and jars were found in Egyptian tombs, but it's too sticky and big for a spice rack.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Ketchup: Ketchup is a sauce, and it likely began as a fermented fish sauce from southern China before tomatoes joined it.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Vinegar: Vinegar is a liquid, and its name comes from the French for 'sour wine'; it keeps in the pantry, not on the spice rack.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Soy sauce: Soy sauce is a bottled liquid, and its brewing is a process that takes months, so it lives in the fridge or pantry.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Olive oil: Olive oil is a cooking fat, and it's best stored away from light and heat, so it doesn't belong on the spice rack.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Oats: Oats are a grain, and they're one of the few foods to carry a heart-health label thanks to a fiber called beta-glucan.
Things you'd find in a spice rack.Yeast: Yeast is a living fungus that eats sugar to make bread rise, so it's kept in the fridge or freezer, not on the spice rack.

Medical instruments.Stethoscope: René Laennec invented it in 1816 to avoid pressing his ear to a patient's chest, using a rolled-up paper tube at first.
Medical instruments.Scalpel: The word comes from Latin for 'little knife', and modern surgical blades are often disposable and extremely sharp.
Medical instruments.Otoscope: It lights up the ear canal and eardrum, and its name comes from the Greek for 'ear'.
Medical instruments.Tongue depressor: This flat wooden stick holds your tongue down for viewing your throat, and crafters buy them as popsicle sticks too.
Medical instruments.Reflex hammer: Doctors tap your knee to test reflexes, and the knee-jerk response is a quick spinal reflex that bypasses the brain.
Medical instruments.Syringe: Its plunger design is an ancient idea, and the hypodermic needle was developed in the 1850s.
Medical instruments.Forceps: Forceps are tongs for gripping tissue, and obstetric forceps have helped deliveries since the 1600s.
Medical instruments.Defibrillator: It shocks a heart out of a chaotic rhythm, and automatic versions now hang in airports and malls.
Medical instruments.Blood pressure cuff: The cuff squeezes your arm to briefly stop blood flow, and your two numbers show pressure at heartbeat and between beats.
Medical instruments.Ophthalmoscope: Helmholtz invented it in 1851, and it lets doctors look through the pupil at the retina and optic nerve.
Medical instruments.Telescope: A trap: it's an optical instrument for distant objects, and not a medical tool, even though it ends in -scope.
Medical instruments.Periscope: A periscope lets you see over obstacles using mirrors, and submarines use them to view the surface.
Medical instruments.Kaleidoscope: Invented by David Brewster in 1816, its name means 'beautiful form viewer' and it uses mirrors for patterns.
Medical instruments.Metronome: A metronome keeps musical tempo, and a doctor's instrument it's not, even though a heartbeat can be like one.
Medical instruments.Barometer: Evangelista Torricelli made the first barometer in 1643, and it measures air pressure, not blood pressure.
Medical instruments.Protractor: A protractor measures angles in geometry, and a doctor would use a goniometer for joint angles instead.
Medical instruments.Gyroscope: A spinning wheel that keeps orientation, used in ships and phones, not in clinics.
Medical instruments.Plunger: A plunger clears drains, and no doctor reaches for one, despite the syringe's resemblance.
Medical instruments.Abacus: An abacus calculates with beads and dates back thousands of years, long before any stethoscope.
Medical instruments.Seismograph: A seismograph records earthquake shaking, so it's an instrument for planets, not patients.
Medical instruments.Spirit level: A spirit level uses a bubble in liquid to show if a surface is flat, a builder's tool.
Medical instruments.Sextant: Sailors used a sextant to measure the angle of stars above the horizon and find their position.
Medical instruments.Compass: A compass points to magnetic north and guides travelers, not diagnoses.
Medical instruments.Hourglass: An hourglass times intervals with sand, and nothing in a doctor's bag resembles it; it measures minutes, not the body.

Skin conditions.Eczema: Eczema is a chronic itchy rash, and it often runs in families with asthma and hay fever.
Skin conditions.Psoriasis: Psoriasis speeds skin cell turnover from about a month to a few days, building up silvery scales, and it isn't contagious.
Skin conditions.Acne: Acne affects most teenagers at some point, and it comes from clogged oil glands rather than dirty skin.
Skin conditions.Hives: Hives are itchy welts from histamine, usually in response to an allergen, and they fade within hours.
Skin conditions.Rosacea: Rosacea causes persistent facial redness, and it's often triggered by spicy food, alcohol or heat.
Skin conditions.Warts: Warts are caused by the human papillomavirus, not toads, and most vanish by themselves with time.
Skin conditions.Sunburn: Sunburn is actually a radiation burn from UV light, and it peels as damaged skin cells are shed.
Skin conditions.Dandruff: Dandruff is partly caused by a yeast living on most scalps, and it isn't from poor hygiene.
Skin conditions.Athlete's foot: A fungus called a dermatophyte causes it, and it loves warm damp shoes and damp locker-room floors.
Skin conditions.Blister: A blister is a fluid cushion that protects damaged skin beneath, which is why you shouldn't pop it.
Skin conditions.Cold sore: Cold sores come from the herpes simplex virus, which stays in your nerves and flares during stress or sun.
Skin conditions.Tinnitus: A trap: tinnitus is ringing in the ears, and nothing to do with skin.
Skin conditions.Glaucoma: Glaucoma is an eye disease that harms the optic nerve.
Skin conditions.Asthma: Asthma is a lung condition, though asthma often goes along with eczema in families.
Skin conditions.Bronchitis: Bronchitis is inflammation of the airways in the lungs, with a lingering cough.
Skin conditions.Gingivitis: Gingivitis is gum disease, in the mouth and not on the skin.
Skin conditions.Arthritis: Arthritis is joint inflammation, though psoriasis can lead to a form called psoriatic arthritis.
Skin conditions.Tonsillitis: Tonsillitis is an infection of the tonsils, a throat issue.
Skin conditions.Cataract: A cataract clouds the lens of the eye, and skin isn't involved.
Skin conditions.Scoliosis: Scoliosis is a curve of the spine, a bone condition rather than a skin one.
Skin conditions.Vertigo: Vertigo is a false sense of spinning from the inner ear.
Skin conditions.Migraine: A migraine is a neurological headache disorder, not a skin one.
Skin conditions.Anemia: Anemia is a shortage of healthy red blood cells, though paleness is a sign you can see on skin.
Skin conditions.Insomnia: Insomnia is trouble sleeping, though a lack of sleep can make skin look dull.

Things you shouldn't microwave.Fork: Metal forks can spark because the tines concentrate electric charge, producing arcs that can damage the oven.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Aluminum foil: Foil's crinkled edges concentrate electric charge and spark, which can start a fire, though a smooth sheet may not.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Metal spoon: A smooth spoon can sometimes survive, but any sharp edge or dent can spark, which is why the rule is no metal at all.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Tin can: A sealed tin can shields its food from microwaves so it won't heat, and the metal can arc too.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Egg in its shell: Steam builds inside the shell faster than it can escape, so the egg can explode, sometimes when you cut into it later.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Smartphone: A phone's metal parts and battery don't mix with microwaves, and the oven will wreck it rather than clean it.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Laptop: A laptop's metal and battery could arc and even catch fire, and microwaves would fry its circuits.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Grapes: Cut a grape almost in half and microwave it, and it can produce a plasma spark show, a famous science trick.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Steel water bottle: Steel reflects microwaves instead of letting them through, so the water inside won't heat and the oven can be damaged.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Butter knife: A knife's metal and edges can make sparks, and that's why the rule is simple: if it's metal, it stays out.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Paper clip: A tiny paper clip still has bent ends that concentrate charge and can spark, ruining the oven.
Things you shouldn't microwave.TV remote: A remote's batteries and tiny circuits can overheat in a microwave, which is why you shouldn't try to disinfect one there.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Popcorn: Popcorn pops because steam builds inside each kernel until the hull bursts, and a built-in patch in the bag helps heat it.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Soup: Soup heats well, but stir it, because a smooth liquid can superheat and then bubble over when disturbed.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Leftovers: Leftovers heat unevenly in a microwave, so stirring or letting them stand helps remove the cold spots where bacteria survive.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Frozen peas: Frozen peas microwave very fast, and a splash of water in a covered bowl steams them nicely.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Mug of tea: Water in a smooth mug can superheat above boiling without bubbling, then erupt when disturbed, so take care.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Oatmeal: Oatmeal microwaves nicely, though it often boils over, so use a bowl much bigger than the portion.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Baked potato: Microwaving a potato works, and piercing the skin first lets steam escape so it doesn't burst.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Rice: Reheated rice can cause food poisoning if left sitting out, because bacterial spores survive cooking, so chill leftovers quickly.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Pizza slice: Leftover pizza often turns rubbery or soggy in the microwave, since steam gets trapped in the crust.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Burrito: Frozen burritos heat unevenly, hot outside and icy inside, which is why wrapping one in a damp paper towel helps.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Pasta: Pasta reheats well in a microwave with a splash of water, since the added steam keeps it from drying out.
Things you shouldn't microwave.Glass of milk: Milk is fine to warm in a microwave, but it can boil over fast, so use short bursts and stir.

Things you don't want to find in your so.Fly: A fly in soup is the stuff of the old joke 'waiter, there's a fly in my soup', one of the most retold restaurant gags.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Hair: Hair in soup is the classic restaurant complaint, and health codes require food workers to wear hair restraints for this reason.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Band-aid: A band-aid in soup is a real cause for food recalls, and many factories use blue plasters so metal detectors can find lost ones.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Sock: A sock in soup is a cartoon nightmare, though 'sock' soup jokes aside, an actual 'stone soup' folk tale begins with just a stone.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Earring: Earrings in soup are a real hazard, and they're easy to lose in a kitchen since small jewelry falls right off while cooking.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Button: A button in soup could crack a tooth, and it's why professional kitchens often ban loose buttons on chef coats.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Spider: A spider in soup is unwelcome, though some people in Cambodia happily eat fried tarantulas as a local snack.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Rubber band: A rubber band in soup shows up in actual food recalls, since elastic bands sneak into packaging lines and processing plants.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Coin: A coin in soup comes from a tradition: bakers and cooks hide a coin in festive dishes, and the lucky finder wins good fortune.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Lego brick: A Lego brick in soup would be a disaster, and fun fact, the bricks are tough enough to survive stomachs, as kids have proven.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Bottle cap: A bottle cap in soup means a factory slip-up, and cap pieces have caused real product recalls over choking hazards.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Battery: A battery in soup is dangerous, since swallowed button batteries can burn the throat in hours and are a medical emergency.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Noodles: Noodles are the star of chicken noodle soup, and the world's oldest known noodles, found in China, are about 4,000 years old.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Carrots: Carrots in soup get their orange from beta-carotene, and until the 1600s many carrots were purple or yellow.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Croutons: Croutons are toasted bread cubes, and they were invented to avoid wasting stale bread, as French cooks did for centuries.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Celery: Celery is part of the classic 'mirepoix' base, which pairs it with onions and carrots, and it's the start of most French soups.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Chicken: Chicken soup is a folk cold remedy, and some lab studies suggest it may mildly calm inflammation, so Grandma had a point.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Lentils: Lentils are among the earliest cultivated crops, with people farming them for roughly 8,000 years, and they cook without soaking.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Onion: Onions are the base of countless soups, and French onion soup became famous as a Parisian late-night meal.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Potatoes: Potatoes in soup were once suspect in Europe, and they only became a staple of dishes like chowder after some centuries.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Peas: Peas make split-pea soup, a dish old enough that ancient Greeks and Romans sold hot pea soup in the street.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Dumplings: Dumplings in soup fit nearly every cuisine, from matzo balls to wontons, which shows how widespread the idea is.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Barley: Barley adds chew to soup, and it is one of the oldest cultivated grains, used in ancient Egypt to make early beer.
Things you don't want to find in your so.Parsley: Parsley is a garnish you may want in soup, and ancient Greeks wore parsley wreaths at events and used it in funerals.

Things a medieval castle has.Moat: A moat is a water-filled ditch around a castle, and it stopped enemies tunneling under walls or rolling siege towers close.
Things a medieval castle has.Drawbridge: A drawbridge could be raised on chains to cut off the entrance, which turned the castle's front door into a blockade.
Things a medieval castle has.Tower: Towers gave defenders height to see and shoot from, and a castle's keep tower was the strongest part.
Things a medieval castle has.Dungeon: A dungeon was originally the keep's main tower, called a donjon, and only later became a name for a prison.
Things a medieval castle has.Throne: A throne room was where the lord held court, and in the hall the lord's seat was set higher than everyone else.
Things a medieval castle has.Great hall: The great hall was the social center, where the whole household ate, and the lord's feasts could last for hours.
Things a medieval castle has.Battlements: Battlements are the notched parapets on top of walls, with gaps called embrasures for archers to shoot through.
Things a medieval castle has.Portcullis: A portcullis is a heavy gate dropped from above, often with iron spikes on the bottom, to trap attackers in the passage.
Things a medieval castle has.Turret: A turret is a small tower on a corner of the wall, and it provided extra angles to see and fire at enemies.
Things a medieval castle has.Courtyard: The courtyard, or bailey, was the open yard where workshops, stables, and daily life took place inside the walls.
Things a medieval castle has.Armory: An armory stored swords, armor, and arms, and knights' plate armor could weigh around 20 to 25 kilograms.
Things a medieval castle has.Elevator: A trap: medieval castles had no elevators, and the first safe passenger elevator was made by Elisha Otis in the 1850s.
Things a medieval castle has.Wi-Fi: Wi-Fi is a 1990s invention, and a castle's communication system was a messenger or a horn.
Things a medieval castle has.Escalator: Escalators date to the 1890s, and a castle's only way up was a narrow stone spiral stair that was easy to defend.
Things a medieval castle has.Garage: Castles had no garages, but they did have stables, and some had a place to keep wagons and siege carts.
Things a medieval castle has.Microwave: A microwave is a 1940s invention, and a medieval castle's kitchen cooked on a huge open hearth.
Things a medieval castle has.Air conditioning: Air conditioning is a 20th-century invention, but thick stone walls helped keep castles cool in summer.
Things a medieval castle has.Solar panels: Solar panels are a modern invention, and castles relied on candles, torches, and fires for light and heat.
Things a medieval castle has.Satellite dish: A satellite dish needs a satellite, and the first one flew in 1957, centuries after castle days.
Things a medieval castle has.Parking lot: A parking lot would have been a field with horses, and castle visitors left their steeds in the stable.
Things a medieval castle has.Movie theater: A movie theater is out of time, and a castle's entertainment was minstrels, jesters, and feasts.
Things a medieval castle has.Vending machine: A vending machine is a modern device, though Hero of Alexandria described a coin-operated holy-water dispenser nearly 2,000 years ago.
Things a medieval castle has.Hot tub: A hot tub is a modern luxury, and medieval castles mostly offered a wooden tub that was filled by hand.
Things a medieval castle has.Doorbell camera: A doorbell camera is modern, and a castle's doorbell was a guard at the gate who shouted his challenge.

Both a food and a color.Orange: The color was named after the fruit in English; before that, English speakers called it geoluhread, meaning yellow-red.
Both a food and a color.Lime: Lime green was named for the fruit, and limes were once given to sailors on British ships to prevent scurvy, hence limeys.
Both a food and a color.Peach: Peach is also a pale pinkish-orange shade; the fruit is native to China, where it symbolises long life.
Both a food and a color.Plum: The deep purple takes its name from the fruit; dried plums are called prunes, and the fruit is one of the first domesticated trees.
Both a food and a color.Cherry: Cherry red is a classic car and lipstick shade; cherries are picked by hand at harvest, and there are hundreds of varieties.
Both a food and a color.Chocolate: Chocolate brown is named for cocoa, which the Aztecs prepared as a bitter, frothy drink rather than a sweet bar.
Both a food and a color.Olive: Olive green is a famous army-uniform shade; olives are bitter straight from the tree and must be cured to be edible.
Both a food and a color.Salmon: Salmon pink is named for the fish's flesh, which is pink because of carotenoid pigments from its diet of krill and shrimp.
Both a food and a color.Mustard: Mustard yellow comes from the seed's colour, and the condiment is among the oldest spices, used since Roman times.
Both a food and a color.Mint: Mint green is a pale cool shade, and the herb's cool feeling comes from menthol, which tricks your cold receptors.
Both a food and a color.Tangerine: Tangerine takes its name from Tangier, Morocco, the port from which the fruit was shipped to Europe in the 1800s.
Both a food and a color.Apricot: Apricot is a soft yellow-orange; the fruit is related to the peach and plum, and the kernel is used to flavour amaretto.
Both a food and a color.Pizza: A trap: pizza is a food but not a color; no common color name comes from it, despite pizza coming in many shades.
Both a food and a color.Bread: Bread is a food, not a color; though 'bread-brown' may seem plausible, no standard color name uses it.
Both a food and a color.Potato: Potatoes are food, not a color; they were first domesticated in the Andes thousands of years ago, in hundreds of hues.
Both a food and a color.Broccoli: Broccoli is food only; 'broccoli green' isn't a standard color, though the vegetable is a human-made cousin of wild cabbage.
Both a food and a color.Pasta: Pasta is only a food; Italians have over 300 shapes of it, but none gives its name to a color.
Both a food and a color.Rice: Rice feeds roughly half the world, but it's a food only here; 'rice' isn't a standard color name like peach or olive.
Both a food and a color.Pretzel: Pretzel is just a food; the twisted shape is said to represent arms crossed in prayer, per a monastic legend.
Both a food and a color.Steak: Steak is a food, not a color; the 'rare', 'medium' and 'well done' terms refer to how long it's cooked.
Both a food and a color.Onion: Onions are only a food here; they come in white, yellow and red, but nobody calls a paint 'onion'.
Both a food and a color.Bagel: Bagel is a food only; they're boiled briefly before baking, which gives them their chewy crust.
Both a food and a color.Waffle: Waffle is a food, not a color; the grid pattern is what makes waffles hold syrup so well.
Both a food and a color.Hot dog: Hot dog is a food, not a color; people eat about 20 billion of them each year in the United States.

Heavy construction vehicles.Bulldozer: A bulldozer pushes soil and rubble with a wide blade, and the name's origin is murky, though bulldoze once meant to intimidate.
Heavy construction vehicles.Excavator: An excavator digs with a boom, stick and bucket on a rotating cab, and the largest mining models weigh hundreds of tonnes.
Heavy construction vehicles.Backhoe: A backhoe has a loader on the front and a digging arm on the back, and is one of the most common machines on small sites.
Heavy construction vehicles.Crane: A crane lifts loads far taller than itself, and a tower crane grows by building itself upward, adding its own sections.
Heavy construction vehicles.Dump truck: A dump truck tips its bed to unload, and the giants in mines carry loads over 300 tonnes, with tyres taller than a person.
Heavy construction vehicles.Cement mixer: A cement mixer keeps its drum turning so concrete doesn't set on the way, and concrete is technically cement mixed with sand and gravel.
Heavy construction vehicles.Steamroller: A steamroller flattens asphalt with a heavy drum, and the name stuck even though modern ones run on diesel, not steam.
Heavy construction vehicles.Grader: A grader levels roads using a long blade slung between the axles, giving a smooth surface for paving.
Heavy construction vehicles.Skid steer: A skid steer turns by running its wheels at different speeds on each side, so it can spin on the spot in tight spaces.
Heavy construction vehicles.Pile driver: A pile driver hammers long posts into the ground to make foundations, and the noise is notorious in cities.
Heavy construction vehicles.Front loader: A front loader scoops and carries piles of material with a big bucket, and it's a typical sight at gravel yards.
Heavy construction vehicles.Combine harvester: A combine harvester cuts, threshes and cleans grain in one pass, so it's heavy farm machinery, not a construction vehicle.
Heavy construction vehicles.Fire engine: A fire engine carries water, ladders and crew, and is an emergency vehicle, not a building machine.
Heavy construction vehicles.Ambulance: An ambulance is built to carry patients quickly, and you'll never see it moving earth.
Heavy construction vehicles.Tank: A tank is a military armoured vehicle on tracks, and tracked tanks and bulldozers look alike, but their jobs are very different.
Heavy construction vehicles.Snowmobile: A snowmobile rides on skis and tracks over snow, and is a recreational vehicle, not a heavy site machine.
Heavy construction vehicles.Golf cart: A golf cart is a small electric vehicle for carrying players, and so far from heavy construction.
Heavy construction vehicles.Monster truck: A monster truck has giant tyres, usually over 1.5 metres tall, but it's built for crushing cars at shows.
Heavy construction vehicles.Zamboni: A Zamboni is an ice resurfacing machine invented by Frank Zamboni in 1949, and is a heavy vehicle, but it's not for construction.
Heavy construction vehicles.Limousine: A limousine is a luxury car with a long body, and so is built for passengers, not heavy work.
Heavy construction vehicles.Tram: A tram runs on tracks through city streets and carries passengers, so it's public transport.
Heavy construction vehicles.Hearse: A hearse is a vehicle that carries a coffin to a funeral, and it's an undertaker's car, not a worksite machine.
Heavy construction vehicles.Ice cream van: An ice cream van plays a tune to attract customers, and it's about as far from heavy machinery as you can get.
Heavy construction vehicles.School bus: A school bus is a large vehicle, painted bright yellow in North America for visibility, but it carries children, not building loads.

Emergency service vehicles.Fire engine: A fire engine strictly means the pumper that carries water and hoses, while the one with the long ladder is a different machine.
Emergency service vehicles.Ambulance: The name comes from the French hopital ambulant, a moving hospital, first used by Napoleon's surgeon Dominique Larrey in the early 1800s.
Emergency service vehicles.Police car: Detroit police pioneered car radios around 1928, which let dispatchers send the nearest patrol car straight to a crime.
Emergency service vehicles.Rescue helicopter: Helicopters can hover over a stricken ship or mountain and lift people out with a winch, reaching places no vehicle can.
Emergency service vehicles.Lifeboat: Britain's lifeboat service, the RNLI, is staffed mostly by volunteers and funded by donations, rather than government money.
Emergency service vehicles.Ladder truck: A ladder truck's aerial ladder can reach over 30 meters on some models, far beyond what a person could carry.
Emergency service vehicles.Air ambulance: Air ambulances cut the trip to a hospital dramatically, which is vital in the golden hour after a serious injury.
Emergency service vehicles.Police motorcycle: Police motorcycles can slip through traffic jams where a car cannot, and are used for escorts and parades.
Emergency service vehicles.Fireboat: Fireboats pump water from the harbor itself, and some can spray tens of thousands of gallons a minute onto waterfront fires.
Emergency service vehicles.Ice cream van: An ice cream van plays a jingle to attract customers, and has nothing to do with emergencies.
Emergency service vehicles.Hearse: A hearse carries a coffin to a funeral, from the French herse, a harrow-shaped frame for candles at funerals.
Emergency service vehicles.Garbage truck: Garbage trucks compact rubbish, and sanitation work is a vital service but not an emergency one.
Emergency service vehicles.School bus: School buses in North America are painted a special yellow, called National School Bus Glossy Yellow, because the color is easy to see.
Emergency service vehicles.Limousine: The limousine is named after the Limousin region in France, where shepherds wore a hooded cloak, and the car's driver compartment was similar.
Emergency service vehicles.Taxi: The word taxi comes from taximeter, the device that measures fares, and a London black cab must have a turning circle of 25 feet.
Emergency service vehicles.Combine harvester: A combine harvester combines reaping, threshing and winnowing in one machine, which is how it got its name.
Emergency service vehicles.Cement mixer: A cement mixer's drum keeps rotating on the road so that the concrete inside doesn't set before it arrives.
Emergency service vehicles.Forklift: A forklift's heavy counterweight at the back stops it tipping forward with a load, and it isn't a road emergency vehicle.
Emergency service vehicles.Double-decker bus: London's red double-decker is iconic, and it carries commuters rather than responding to emergencies.
Emergency service vehicles.Rickshaw: The word rickshaw comes from the Japanese jinrikisha, meaning human-powered vehicle, and is still a taxi in many cities.
Emergency service vehicles.Go-kart: The first go-kart was built in 1956 in California by Art Ingels, from lawnmower engine parts.
Emergency service vehicles.Zamboni: The Zamboni ice resurfacer is named after Frank Zamboni, who invented it in 1949 in California to smooth his skating rink.
Emergency service vehicles.Camper van: A camper van is a home on wheels for vacations, with a bed and kitchen, not an emergency vehicle.
Emergency service vehicles.Food truck: Food trucks trace back to the chuck wagon, invented in 1866 by the cattle rancher Charles Goodnight.

macOS versions named after California pl.Yosemite: OS X Yosemite (2014) took its name from the national park known for El Capitan and Half Dome. It brought a flatter, lighter design.
macOS versions named after California pl.El Capitan: El Capitan, a giant granite wall in Yosemite popular with climbers, gave its name to the 2015 release, a refinement of Yosemite.
macOS versions named after California pl.Sierra: macOS Sierra (2016) is named for the Sierra Nevada mountains. It was also the first release to bring Siri to the Mac.
macOS versions named after California pl.High Sierra: macOS High Sierra (2017) is named for the high-elevation Sierra Nevada. It introduced the modern Apple File System.
macOS versions named after California pl.Mojave: macOS Mojave (2018) honors the Mojave Desert and introduced a system-wide Dark Mode. Apple often uses the desert's landscapes in its wallpapers.
macOS versions named after California pl.Catalina: macOS Catalina (2019) refers to Santa Catalina Island off the Los Angeles coast. It ended iTunes by splitting it into separate apps.
macOS versions named after California pl.Big Sur: macOS Big Sur (2020) is named for a dramatic stretch of California coast. It was a major redesign and moved the Mac to a new version number, 11.
macOS versions named after California pl.Monterey: macOS Monterey (2021) is named for the coastal city and bay of Monterey, home to a famed aquarium. It brought Shortcuts to the Mac.
macOS versions named after California pl.Ventura: macOS Ventura (2022) takes its name from the coastal city and county north of Los Angeles. It introduced Stage Manager.
macOS versions named after California pl.Sonoma: macOS Sonoma (2023) is named for the wine region north of San Francisco. It introduced desktop widgets and screensavers.
macOS versions named after California pl.Sequoia: macOS Sequoia (2024) honors the giant redwood trees and their national park. It brought iPhone mirroring to the Mac.
macOS versions named after California pl.Tahoe: macOS Tahoe (2025) is named for the big alpine lake on the California-Nevada border. It was the last version to support Intel Macs.
macOS versions named after California pl.Tiger: Mac OS X Tiger (2005) is one of the big-cat names Apple used before Mavericks. It's a real animal, not a California place.
macOS versions named after California pl.Leopard: Mac OS X Leopard (2007) belongs to the earlier big-cat series. It's a wildcat, not a Californian location.
macOS versions named after California pl.Lion: OS X Lion (2011) came near the end of the cat-themed names. A lion is an animal, not a California place.
macOS versions named after California pl.Panther: Mac OS X Panther (2003) was one of Apple's early cat names. It isn't a place in California.
macOS versions named after California pl.Jaguar: Mac OS X Jaguar (2002) was the third release of Mac OS X and part of the big-cat era. Not a California name.
macOS versions named after California pl.Cheetah: Mac OS X 10.0 Cheetah, released in 2001, was the very first version of Mac OS X. It's a cat, not a place.

Real internet domain endings..com: Short for commercial, it is the most used ending; the first .com ever registered was symbolics.com in 1985.
Real internet domain endings..org: Originally meant for nonprofits, it hosts Wikipedia and countless charities, though anyone can register one.
Real internet domain endings..net: Short for network, it was meant for internet infrastructure firms, but today anyone can buy one.
Real internet domain endings..edu: Reserved for accredited US colleges and universities, which is why it is such a clear marker of American education.
Real internet domain endings..gov: Restricted to US government bodies; other countries use second-level forms such as .gov.uk.
Real internet domain endings..io: It is really the code for the British Indian Ocean Territory, but startups love it because 'io' means input/output.
Real internet domain endings..uk: The UK's country code is .uk, not .gb, even though GB is the country's official ISO code.
Real internet domain endings..de: Germany's country code is one of the largest in the world, with well over 15 million registrations.
Real internet domain endings..ai: Anguilla's country code has become a goldmine for the tiny Caribbean island thanks to the artificial intelligence boom.
Real internet domain endings..tv: This belongs to the island nation of Tuvalu, which earns notable income by leasing it to video sites.
Real internet domain endings..info: Launched in 2001 as the first open alternative to .com, it carries no restrictions on who can register.
Real internet domain endings..biz: Introduced in 2001 for businesses, it never came close to dislodging .com, which most firms still prefer.
Real internet domain endings..co: Colombia's country code, marketed worldwide as a short form of company or commerce.
Real internet domain endings..www: Here 'www' is just a hostname prefix in addresses such as www.example.com, not an ending.
Real internet domain endings..http: Http names the protocol that comes before '://' in an address; it is never a domain ending.
Real internet domain endings..html: A file extension for web pages, found at the end of a file path, not a top-level domain.
Real internet domain endings..exe: A Windows program file extension, which you may spot in a download link but never as a domain ending.
Real internet domain endings..jpg: An image file extension; it appears after a filename, not after the domain.
Real internet domain endings..usa: The US country code is just .us, so .usa does not exist.
Real internet domain endings..pdf: A document file extension from Adobe's format; it's a file type, not a domain.
Real internet domain endings..cmo: A mistyped .com. The real .cm belongs to Cameroon, and scammers cash in on .com typos with it.
Real internet domain endings..txt: A plain-text file extension; robots.txt is a famous example telling search engines where not to go.
Real internet domain endings..ftp: FTP is a file transfer protocol that appears before the address as ftp://, not as an ending.
Real internet domain endings..orgg: A typo of .org with a doubled g; no such ending exists, though typosquatters love lookalike addresses.

Pokémon items.Poké Ball: The name comes from pocket monster ball, and in the games the capture odds depend partly on how weakened the target is.
Pokémon items.Master Ball: It never fails to catch a Pokemon, and in most games you receive only one, so players agonize over when to use it.
Pokémon items.Great Ball: A step above the basic Poke Ball, it improves catch odds by about one and a half times.
Pokémon items.Ultra Ball: It catches at about twice the rate of a Poke Ball, and it's the strongest ball you can buy in most games.
Pokémon items.Potion: A basic healing item that restores 20 HP, and it's usually the first healing item players use.
Pokémon items.Super Potion: The upgrade over the basic Potion, restoring a larger amount of HP, so it's a typical mid-game purchase.
Pokémon items.Rare Candy: Raises a Pokemon's level by exactly one, handy for skipping tedious training, and it's often hidden in dungeons.
Pokémon items.Revive: Brings a fainted Pokemon back into the fight with half its HP, so it's essential after a tough battle.
Pokémon items.Escape Rope: Teleports you straight out of a cave or dungeon back to its entrance, a cheap way to avoid the walk.
Pokémon items.Fire Stone: Evolves Vulpix, Growlithe and Eevee, which becomes Flareon when exposed to it.
Pokémon items.Thunder Stone: Evolves Pikachu into Raichu, a choice many players hesitate over because it permanently changes the mascot.
Pokémon items.Moon Stone: Evolves Clefairy and Jigglypuff, which were among the first Pokemon that evolved using stones.
Pokémon items.Repel: Keeps weaker wild Pokemon from appearing for a while, so you can walk through tall grass without battles.
Pokémon items.Phoenix Down: A trap: it revives KO'd party members in Final Fantasy, whereas Pokemon's equivalent is called Revive.
Pokémon items.Rupee: A trap: rupees are Zelda's money, and you'd spend them on bombs and shields, not in a Pokemon game.
Pokémon items.Super Mushroom: A trap: it's the Super Mario power-up that makes Mario grow bigger, not a Pokemon item.
Pokémon items.Fire Flower: A trap: it gives Mario fireballs, and it's a Mario item rather than a Pokemon one.
Pokémon items.Heart Container: A trap: it adds a heart to Link's health in Zelda, which isn't how Pokemon health works.
Pokémon items.Estus Flask: A trap: it's the refillable healing flask of Dark Souls, so it doesn't belong in Pokemon.
Pokémon items.Triforce: A trap: it's the Zelda triangle of power, wisdom and courage, rather than something you'd find in Pokemon.
Pokémon items.Master Sword: A trap: it's Link's blade in Zelda; Pokemon has a Master Ball, which makes the confusion tempting but wrong.
Pokémon items.Chaos Emerald: A trap: Sonic's seven gems; both series involve collectibles, but these gems are Sonic's.
Pokémon items.Senzu Bean: A trap: it's a healing bean from Dragon Ball that restores energy instantly, not a Pokemon item.
Pokémon items.Power Pellet: A trap: Pac-Man's large dots let him eat ghosts for a short time, and they aren't in Pokemon.

Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Hansel and Gretel: Grimm tales were first written for scholars, not children; this one has a witch's cottage made of bread and sweets and a clever escape.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Rapunzel: The Grimm version has a prince blinded by thorns; a tower-locked girl is named after a salad plant, rampion.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Rumpelstiltskin: The Grimms collected this tale of a gnome who spins gold for a price, and it was one of their best-known stories.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Snow White: In the Grimms' 1812 original, the villain is the girl's own mother; Disney's 1937 film was the first full-length cel-animated feature.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.The Frog Prince: In the Grimms' version, the princess flings the frog against a wall, instead of kissing him, to break the spell.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.The Golden Goose: A story about a golden-feathered bird that makes everyone who touches it stick, collected by the Grimms.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Mother Holle: When she shakes her featherbed, it snows on Earth; this Grimm tale rewards kind work and punishes laziness.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.The Goose Girl: A princess is cheated of her place by her maid, and finds help from a talking horse's head; a Grimm tale.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Brave Little Tailor: A tailor who killed seven flies with one blow becomes a hero in this Grimm story, which has a 'Seven at one blow' belt.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Iron John: A wild man locked in a cage becomes a loyal helper to a prince in this less-famous Grimm tale, retold by poet Robert Bly.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Briar Rose: The Grimms' name for Sleeping Beauty, whose thorny-rose hedge guards a castle; the curse comes from a spindle.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.The Little Mermaid: Hans Christian Andersen's 1837 tale about a girl who gave up her voice, from Denmark, not the Brothers Grimm.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.The Ugly Duckling: Andersen's Danish tale about a swan raised by ducks is not a Grimm story.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.The Snow Queen: Andersen's story of a boy and the ice-shard mirror inspired Disney's Frozen, and is not Grimm.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Thumbelina: A tiny girl from a flower is Andersen's creation, not a Grimm tale.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Goldilocks: This English tale was first published in 1837 by Robert Southey; it's not a Grimm.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Three Little Pigs: An English folk tale, with a wolf huffing and puffing; it is not by the Grimms.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Aladdin: A tale from the Arabian Nights, though the lamp-and-genie story was added to it later by Antoine Galland in 1700s France.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Pinocchio: Collodi's Italian novel about a wooden puppet is not a Grimm tale.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Peter Pan: J. M. Barrie's 1904 play is about a boy who never grows up, and is not a Grimm tale.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Little Match Girl: Andersen's 1845 tale of a child selling matches is not a Grimm story.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.The Red Shoes: Andersen wrote about the cursed shoes, not the Grimms.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.Beauty and the Beast: The 1740 French tale by Gabrielle-Suzanne de Villeneuve, shortened by Beaumont, is not Grimm.
Tales collected by the Brothers Grimm.The Nightingale: Andersen's story of a mechanical and a real bird is a Danish tale, not Grimm.

Literary devices.Alliteration: "Peter Piper picked a peck" is the tongue-twister, but poets from Beowulf on used repeated sounds as a core structure.
Literary devices.Metaphor: From Greek "to carry across", Shakespeare's "All the world's a stage" is a famous extended one.
Literary devices.Simile: It compares using "like" or "as", as in Burns's "My love is like a red, red rose", unlike a metaphor.
Literary devices.Hyperbole: From Greek for "overshooting", it's behind "I've told you a million times", which most people say weekly.
Literary devices.Onomatopoeia: Words like "buzz" and "sizzle" imitate sounds, though languages differ: English dogs say woof, Japanese dogs say wan-wan.
Literary devices.Personification: Giving human traits to non-human things, as in "the wind howled", which poets rely on constantly.
Literary devices.Irony: Oedipus Rex is a classic example of dramatic irony: the audience knows what the hero doesn't.
Literary devices.Foreshadowing: Hints of what's to come, as in Chekhov's gun: a gun on the wall in act one must be fired by act three.
Literary devices.Oxymoron: The word itself is an oxymoron, from Greek "sharp-dull", and "deafening silence" is another.
Literary devices.Assonance: Repeating vowel sounds within nearby words, as in "the rain in Spain stays mainly in the plain".
Literary devices.Allegory: A story whose characters stand for ideas, as in Orwell's Animal Farm, which retells the Russian Revolution.
Literary devices.Synecdoche: A part stands for the whole, as "wheels" for a car or "all hands on deck", from Greek for "taking together".
Literary devices.Anaphora: Repeating the start of successive clauses for effect, as in "I have a dream" in King's speech.
Literary devices.Chiaroscuro: A painting term for light-dark contrast. Writers borrow it, but it isn't a literary device.
Literary devices.Sfumato: Leonardo's smoky blending of tones, from Italian for "smoked", is a painting technique rather than a literary one.
Literary devices.Impasto: Thickly applied paint that holds the brush's texture, a painter's term and not a writer's, however textured prose is.
Literary devices.Fresco: Painting on wet plaster, as in the Sistine Chapel ceiling, an art method rather than a literary device.
Literary devices.Crescendo: A music term for growing gradually louder, not a literary device, though writers use the word loosely.
Literary devices.Staccato: Short, detached notes in music, from Italian for "detached", so a musical term, not a literary one.
Literary devices.Fortissimo: Very loud in music, marked ff, a term for dynamics in a score and not a term for literature.
Literary devices.Pirouette: A ballet spin on one foot, from French for "spinning top", so a dance term, not a literary one.
Literary devices.Plié: A ballet bend of the knees, from French for "bent", and a dance move rather than a figure of speech.
Literary devices.Glissando: A slide between notes, as in the famous clarinet opening of Rhapsody in Blue, so it's a music term.
Literary devices.Tempera: Egg-yolk paint used by painters for centuries, so it's an art medium and not a literary device.

Things visible at night with the naked e.The Moon: The Moon is always showing the same face to Earth, and you can see its dark maria, ancient lava plains, without binoculars.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Venus: Venus is the brightest planet and often called the evening or morning star, but it is a scorching world with an acid-cloud sky.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Mars: Mars looks reddish because of iron oxide dust on its surface, and its brightness varies a lot over its orbit.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Jupiter: Jupiter is the largest planet, and in good conditions its brightness exceeds almost every star in the sky.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Saturn: Saturn shines as a steady yellowish point, but you need a small telescope to see its rings.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Shooting star: A shooting star is a meteor, usually a grain of dust or sand burning up about 100 kilometers above you.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Milky Way: The Milky Way is our own galaxy seen edge-on, with more than 100 billion stars, visible as a hazy band under dark skies.
Things visible at night with the naked e.ISS: The International Space Station is visible as a fast-moving bright light, and it orbits Earth about every 90 minutes.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Big Dipper: The Big Dipper is part of Ursa Major, and its two outer stars point toward Polaris.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Orion's Belt: Orion's Belt is three stars in a row, and it's visible from nearly everywhere on Earth.
Things visible at night with the naked e.North Star: Polaris, the North Star, sits almost directly above the North Pole, so it appears to stay still while others circle.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Neptune: Neptune is too dim for the naked eye, and it was found in 1846 using mathematical predictions before it was seen.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Black hole: A black hole emits no light of its own, so you can't see one with the naked eye, only its effects.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Pluto: Pluto is far too faint to see without a good telescope, and it was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Proxima Centauri: Proxima Centauri is the closest star to the Sun but too faint for naked-eye viewing, as it is a small red dwarf.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Rainbow: A rainbow needs sunlight and rain, so it is a daytime sight, though a faint moonbow can appear at night.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Dark matter: Dark matter doesn't emit or reflect light, so it can only be detected by its gravitational effects.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Ozone layer: The ozone layer is invisible to the eye, and it blocks most of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Exoplanet: Exoplanets orbit other stars and are too faint and close to their stars to see without powerful telescopes.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Sunspots: Sunspots are visible only in the daytime with proper solar filters, and they are cooler patches on the Sun.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Gravity: Gravity can't be seen at all, only observed through its effects, such as the Moon's orbit.
Things visible at night with the naked e.X-rays: X-rays are invisible to human eyes, and astronomers must use space telescopes to see X-ray sources.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Ceres: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt, and it's too dim to see without a telescope or binoculars.
Things visible at night with the naked e.Radio waves: Radio waves are invisible, and radio telescopes pick up signals from distant galaxies.

Places where aircraft land or park.Runway: Runways are numbered by compass heading divided by ten, so runway 27 points due west, at 270 degrees.
Places where aircraft land or park.Hangar: Hangar is thought to come from an old French word for an enclosure; it was borrowed for aircraft shelters in the early 1900s.
Places where aircraft land or park.Airstrip: Remote bush airstrips in Alaska, Papua New Guinea and Australia are lifelines, sometimes just a cleared stretch of grass or gravel.
Places where aircraft land or park.Helipad: Helipads are marked with a big H, usually inside a circle, so pilots can pick them out from above.
Places where aircraft land or park.Aircraft carrier: A US supercarrier's steam catapult can fling a jet from a standstill to around 150 mph in about two seconds.
Places where aircraft land or park.Airfield: Many wartime British airfields were simply grass fields, and a few of those, such as Duxford, still host flying displays today.
Places where aircraft land or park.Aerodrome: Aerodrome is older than airport, and it still appears in aviation rules and on place names in Britain and Canada.
Places where aircraft land or park.Apron: The apron is the paved area where planes park, board and refuel, kept separate from the taxiways and runways.
Places where aircraft land or park.Airbase: Ramstein in Germany is among the largest US Air Force bases outside the United States, home to thousands of personnel.
Places where aircraft land or park.Heliport: São Paulo has long been famous for rooftop heliports, since many wealthy residents commute by helicopter above the traffic.
Places where aircraft land or park.Depot: Buses and trains are parked and serviced at a depot, but not aircraft; planes use hangars and aprons instead.
Places where aircraft land or park.Garage: A garage houses cars, though in British English the same word also means a petrol station; planes need a hangar.
Places where aircraft land or park.Station: A station is for trains, or crews like the fire brigade; aircraft don't dock at one, though a helicopter might use a heliport.
Places where aircraft land or park.Stable: Stables are for horses, not aircraft, though a few early aeroplanes were stored in horse stables at country estates.
Places where aircraft land or park.Shipyard: Ships are built and repaired at a shipyard; the only aircraft there would be a helicopter passing over.
Places where aircraft land or park.Dry dock: A dry dock is a basin drained to work on ships' hulls; it parks vessels, not aircraft, even if carriers use them.
Places where aircraft land or park.Bus stop: Bus stops are for passengers boarding buses; aircraft only stop at gates or stands.
Places where aircraft land or park.Car park: A car park holds vehicles, but not aircraft, though some airports use multi-storey ones right beside the terminal.
Places where aircraft land or park.Siding: A siding is a short rail track off the main line where trains wait; planes never park there.
Places where aircraft land or park.Velodrome: A velodrome is a banked cycling track that can reach about 42 degrees at its steepest; no aircraft land on one.
Places where aircraft land or park.Paddock: A paddock is a small field for horses, or the area where racehorses or race cars are prepared; it is not for aircraft.
Places where aircraft land or park.Bike rack: A bike rack holds bicycles, not aircraft, though the world's largest bike parking, in Utrecht, holds over 12,000 of them.
Places where aircraft land or park.Taxi rank: Taxi ranks are where cabs queue for fares; aircraft also "taxi", but along taxiways, not ranks.
Places where aircraft land or park.Lay-by: A lay-by is a roadside bay for stopping vehicles; a road, though, can double as an emergency runway in some countries like Finland.

Valentine's Day things.Cupid: The Roman god of desire, called Eros in Greek myth, is shown as a winged boy. In early art he was a handsome adult.
Valentine's Day things.Red rose: Red roses symbolize romantic love. About 250 million roses are grown for Valentine's Day each year.
Valentine's Day things.Heart: The heart shape doesn't look much like the real organ. It may come from an ancient plant seed, silphium, used as a contraceptive.
Valentine's Day things.Love letter: The oldest known Valentine message is a poem written in 1415 by the Duke of Orléans to his wife from the Tower of London.
Valentine's Day things.Box of chocolates: Richard Cadbury introduced the first heart-shaped chocolate box for Valentine's Day in the 1860s.
Valentine's Day things.Valentine card: Handmade valentines grew into a huge business in the 1800s. The US now sees over a hundred million exchanged each year.
Valentine's Day things.Teddy bear: Teddy bears are named after US president Theodore Roosevelt, after a 1902 hunting trip where he refused to shoot a captured bear.
Valentine's Day things.Candlelit dinner: Candles give a soft glow that flatters faces, which is why a candlelit dinner is a classic romantic move.
Valentine's Day things.Bow and arrow: Cupid's arrows are said to make people fall in love. In myth, he carried golden ones for love and leaden ones for indifference.
Valentine's Day things.Lovebirds: Lovebirds are small parrots that form strong pair bonds, and they often sit close in pairs.
Valentine's Day things.Shamrock: This three-leaf clover is Ireland's emblem, tied to St. Patrick's Day in March, not to the February romance of Valentine's.
Valentine's Day things.Pumpkin: Pumpkins belong to autumn: Halloween carving and Thanksgiving pie. February is far outside their harvest season.
Valentine's Day things.Mistletoe: Mistletoe is the Christmas kissing plant. It's tempting as a romance symbol, but it's a December tradition, not February.
Valentine's Day things.Dreidel: This four-sided spinning top is a Hanukkah game, played in December with chocolate coins or nuts as stakes.
Valentine's Day things.Egg hunt: Hiding and finding eggs is an Easter ritual in spring, with no link to the February 14 holiday of romance.
Valentine's Day things.Firecracker: Firecrackers are for Chinese New Year and the Fourth of July, where noise is meant to scare off bad luck or celebrate independence.
Valentine's Day things.Turkey: The Thanksgiving centerpiece. Americans eat about 45 million turkeys at the November holiday, none of them romantic.
Valentine's Day things.Maypole: Dancers weave ribbons around a maypole on May Day, celebrating spring. It is not a Valentine's custom.
Valentine's Day things.Bonfire: Bonfires light up Guy Fawkes Night and midsummer festivals, not the quiet candlelit romance of Valentine's Day.
Valentine's Day things.Witch: Witches are Halloween icons, riding brooms in October. They don't fit a holiday of hearts and flowers.
Valentine's Day things.Candy corn: This tri-color sweet is a Halloween staple, sold in autumn, while Valentine's Day candy is usually conversation hearts.
Valentine's Day things.Lantern: Lanterns light up the Chinese Lantern Festival and mid-autumn celebrations, not Valentine's Day.
Valentine's Day things.Green beer: Beer dyed green is a St. Patrick's Day custom in March, mostly American, and has nothing to do with Valentine's Day.
Valentine's Day things.Tinsel: Tinsel hangs on Christmas trees in December. Valentine's decor leans toward red hearts and paper cutouts.

Christian holidays and seasons.Christmas: Celebrated on 25 December, it was fixed as a date in the 4th century, and the Western date differs from the Orthodox 7 January.
Christian holidays and seasons.Easter: The date of Easter moves each year, falling on the first Sunday after the first full moon after the spring equinox.
Christian holidays and seasons.Good Friday: The day marks the crucifixion, and despite its name, 'good' likely meant holy, as in the old sense of the word.
Christian holidays and seasons.Lent: The 40-day season of fasting before Easter does not count Sundays, so it lasts longer than forty calendar days.
Christian holidays and seasons.Advent: The four-week period before Christmas is the start of the church year, and its name comes from the Latin for coming.
Christian holidays and seasons.Epiphany: Celebrated on 6 January, it marks the visit of the Magi and ends the twelve days of Christmas.
Christian holidays and seasons.Pentecost: Held fifty days after Easter, the name comes from the Greek for fiftieth, and it is called the church's birthday.
Christian holidays and seasons.Ash Wednesday: Ashes are marked on foreheads, and the ashes traditionally come from burning the previous year's palm branches.
Christian holidays and seasons.All Saints' Day: Celebrated on 1 November, it honours all saints, and Halloween is named after its eve.
Christian holidays and seasons.Palm Sunday: The Sunday before Easter commemorates Jesus's entry into Jerusalem, and it starts Holy Week.
Christian holidays and seasons.Maundy Thursday: This is the Thursday before Easter, remembering the Last Supper, and its name comes from the Latin word for commandment.
Christian holidays and seasons.Hanukkah: Hanukkah is a Jewish festival of lights, which lasts eight nights and recalls the rededication of the Temple.
Christian holidays and seasons.Passover: Passover is Jewish, and the Last Supper may have been a Passover meal, which creates a link but it is not Christian.
Christian holidays and seasons.Diwali: Diwali is the Hindu festival of lights, celebrated by Sikhs and Jains as well.
Christian holidays and seasons.Ramadan: Ramadan is the Islamic holy month of fasting, and it is not a Christian season.
Christian holidays and seasons.Eid al-Fitr: Eid al-Fitr is an Islamic holiday that ends the Ramadan fast.
Christian holidays and seasons.Yom Kippur: Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, is the holiest day in Judaism.
Christian holidays and seasons.Holi: Holi is a Hindu spring festival of colours, which is no Christian occasion.
Christian holidays and seasons.Vesak: Vesak marks the birth, enlightenment and death of the Buddha, and is a Buddhist holiday.
Christian holidays and seasons.Purim: Purim is a Jewish holiday remembering the Persian Jews' rescue, and people dress up in costumes.
Christian holidays and seasons.Kwanzaa: Kwanzaa was created in 1966 by Maulana Karenga and is celebrated by African Americans from 26 December to 1 January.
Christian holidays and seasons.Navratri: Navratri is a Hindu festival of nine nights honouring the goddess Durga.
Christian holidays and seasons.Sukkot: Sukkot is a Jewish harvest festival where people build and eat in temporary huts.
Christian holidays and seasons.Rosh Hashanah: Rosh Hashanah is the Jewish New Year and is celebrated with apples and honey.

Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Turkey: About 46 million turkeys are eaten on US Thanksgiving, and Benjamin Franklin supposedly preferred them to the bald eagle as a national bird, though that's often exaggerated.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Stuffing: Called dressing in parts of the South, it dates to Roman cookbooks that stuffed birds with herbs, nuts and cooked grains.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Cranberry sauce: Cranberries are one of only three major fruits native to North America, along with blueberries and Concord grapes.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Mashed potatoes: Potatoes were an Andean crop, brought to Europe in the 1500s, so Pilgrims probably didn't have them at the first feast.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Gravy: Made from pan drippings, gravy is often the very thing that dry turkey is rescued by.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Pumpkin pie: The pumpkin is a native American squash; the earliest recorded recipes in English cookbooks predate the 1700s.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Sweet potatoes: The topping of marshmallow began as a 1917 advertising campaign by a marshmallow company.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Green bean casserole: It was invented in 1955 by a Campbell's Soup test kitchen worker, Dorcas Reilly, using cream of mushroom soup and fried onions.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Cornbread: Corn was the staple grain Native Americans taught colonists to grow and prepare, and cornbread is its descendant.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Dinner rolls: Bread rolls are a Thanksgiving side to mop up gravy, probably appearing at most tables.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Pecan pie: The pecan is native to North America; the pie is especially linked to the American South, and its corn syrup became popular in the 1930s.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Corn: Thanksgiving's old centerpiece was the native crop corn, and Native American farmers had grown it for thousands of years.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Yule log: A chocolate Christmas dessert from France, with the name derived from the old Yule log burned at midwinter.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Hot cross buns: Spiced buns marked with a cross, eaten at Easter time and on Good Friday.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Latkes: Hanukkah potato pancakes, fried in oil to remember the temple oil miracle.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Candy canes: A Christmas sweet, said to be bent into a shepherd's crook shape, though that story is a legend.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Gingerbread house: A Christmas craft inspired by Hansel and Gretel, and not Thanksgiving.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Haggis: Scotland's national dish, sheep's offal with oatmeal in a stomach casing, is honoured on Burns Night.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Pavlova: A meringue dessert named after the dancer Anna Pavlova, which Australia and New Zealand both claim; it's served at Christmas there.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Matzo ball soup: A Passover and Jewish staple, whose dumplings are made of matzo meal.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Fruitcake: A British Christmas cake that keeps for months thanks to alcohol and sugar, famously said to last for years.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Chili: A spicy stew dear to Texans, it's not a standard Thanksgiving plate.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Lasagna: Layered Italian pasta, a classic Italian-American feast but not a Thanksgiving tradition.
Classic American Thanksgiving dishes.Fish and chips: The British takeaway classic, deep-fried fish with chips, isn't on a Thanksgiving table.

Soviet space program (not NASA).Yuri Gagarin: On 12 April 1961 he became the first human in space, completing one orbit of Earth in about 108 minutes.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Tereshkova: Valentina Tereshkova flew in 1963 as the first woman in space, and remains the only woman to have flown a solo space mission.

Soviet space program (not NASA).Luna 2: In 1959 it became the first human-made object to reach the Moon, crashing deliberately onto its surface.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Salyut: Salyut 1, launched in 1971, was the world's first space station, preceding NASA's Skylab.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Mir: The Russian station was in orbit for 15 years from 1986 and was deliberately brought down into the Pacific in 2001.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Soyuz: First flown in the 1960s, this spacecraft design is still used today to carry crews to the International Space Station.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Venera: These Soviet probes performed the first landings on Venus, where the hostile surface destroyed them within about an hour or two.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Lunokhod: Lunokhod 1 in 1970 was the first remote-controlled rover on another world, and drove over 10 kilometres on the Moon.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Alan Shepard: He was America's first man in space in 1961, a flight lasting only about 15 minutes, a month after Gagarin.
Soviet space program (not NASA).John Glenn: The first American to orbit Earth in 1962, he returned to space at age 77 in 1998 aboard a shuttle.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Neil Armstrong: He was the first person to walk on the Moon in July 1969, an American achievement under NASA's Apollo program.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Explorer 1: America's first satellite, launched in 1958, discovered the Van Allen radiation belts.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Mercury: NASA's first human spaceflight program, it flew from 1961 to 1963 with single-astronaut capsules.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Gemini: NASA's two-person program of the mid-1960s tested spacewalks and orbital docking in preparation for the Moon.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Skylab: America's first space station was launched in 1973, two years after the Soviet Salyut 1.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Voyager: NASA's twin probes launched in 1977 and became the first human-made objects to enter interstellar space.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Sally Ride: She became the first American woman in space in 1983, on a NASA shuttle mission.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Ham the chimp: This chimpanzee flew a NASA Mercury suborbital flight in January 1961, a few months before Alan Shepard.
Soviet space program (not NASA).Pioneer: NASA's Pioneer probes carried plaques showing humans and Earth's location, in case aliens found them.
